The Italian government coalition has split over the military aid to Ukraine, just after Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni secured a seat for Rome in the peace talks session in Abu Dhabi.

On Tuesday 10 November the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine is presented to Copasir (Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic) by Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, but League Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti is biding his time over signing the new measure, as the procedure would require.

Within the governing majority, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Crosetto himself tend to play down the incident, citing the minister's absence, as on Monday he had been in Brussels for Ecofin. Tajani goes so far as to specify that, since the document is classified, it has to be signed in person and cannot be signed electronically.

Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has also spoken about Italian and European strategy for Ukraine, in an interview with the daily newspaper Repubblica (source in Italian). The Defence chief, who says he is convinced that Giorgetti will sign the aid package as soon as he returns from Brussels, has defended the need to continue supporting Kyiv.

He also stressed the need for Europe to maintain a common position, as requested by Meloni, and reiterated that "excluding a physical presence in Ukraine of European troops has always been our caveat". Sources at Palazzo Chigi reiterate the point even after the start of talks in Abu Dhabi: "Europe must speak with a single voice and equip itself with a clear and shared mandate".

The row has broken out, however, because Deputy Prime Minister and Infrastructure Minister Matteo Salvini has repeatedly voiced his reservations about military aid to Kyiv, despite Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has always remained firm (together with FI) on the need to continue supporting Kyiv "for as long as necessary".

A line that has become tighter after the League congress that reconfirmed him as secretary. League senator Claudio Borghi, in fact, steps up the pressure on X, calling the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine the "decree that does not exist (because an act that requires joint approval by several ministers does not exist until it has been signed by them)".

Without the signature of League minister Giorgetti, the decree cannot be published and the aid, not only military but also civilian, cannot be sent. This risks opening a delicate battle within the majority on this issue, which could turn into a clash whose consequences are still hard to make out.

What could be in the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine

On the list of measures in the decree (classified like all the previous ones) there will in fact not only be aid for Ukrainian civilians, such as generators, but probably also weapons for air defence. Since the Franco-Italian Samp-T battery has already been supplied in the past, there could therefore be a shipment of Aster missiles that arm the system.

Within the majority, many are convinced that in the end the minister will sign, also because otherwise the experience of the centre-right government would come dangerously close to the end of the line. A scenario that could prove catastrophic, not only for the European balance. The Italian government is in the middle of the budget session and a crisis at this point would risk sweeping away the budget plan as well.

Why the so-called framework decree introduced by Draghi is important

Moreover, the decree-law that serves as a "framework" for this mechanism, which then provides for the ministerial decree with the joint approval of Defence, Farnesina and the Economy and Finance Ministry, will also expire at the end of the year. This is a scheme introduced by the Draghi government in 2022 and already renewed four times with only a few small adjustments, regardless of the governing majority.

After being adopted in the Council of Ministers, those framework decrees were converted into law by the Houses of Parliament, allowing in four years the dispatch of twelve military aid packages through as many interministerial measures, for which only a briefing to the Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic is required.

The last aid package to Kyiv was sent at the end of 2025. A few days after Christmas last year, now eleven months ago, the government adopted a new "framework" decree that authorises the shipment of supplies, both military and civilian, to Ukraine for the whole of 2026.

Moscow’s list of states it deems unfriendly was set in March 2022 for foreign economic policy, but decrees and court rulings now apply it to child custody, vehicle registration and debt repayment.

Russia's designation of "unfriendly countries" has expanded beyond foreign economic policy into domestic courts, family law, property rights and financial obligations, with a string of decrees and rulings extending its reach to individuals.

The list of states Moscow considers unfriendly was formalised as a form of retaliation in a government order in March 2022, weeks after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

It covers the US, the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Ukraine, Australia, New Zealand and EU member states, all of which have pushed back against Russia's war of aggression.

This autumn, the Russian government nearly doubled import duties on spirits from unfriendly countries, raising the rate from 20% to 35%, primarily affecting European and North American producers.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the placement of foreign companies' Russian assets under temporary administration was directly linked to those companies' home countries being on the list.

The measure has affected the Russian operations of Nestlé, Auchan, FM Logistic, Leroy Merlin, Metro Cash & Carry, Tarkett, Japan Tobacco International (JTI) and others.

Russia's Supreme Court cited the unfriendly countries designation in a child custody dispute, ruling that returning a child to France could run counter to her interests in part because France appears on the list.

In March 2025, Russian citizen Alexei Ermakov took his daughter on a two-week holiday to Turkey and Slovakia with the consent of her mother, Ukrainian citizen Anna Tishkova, then brought the child to Russia in April.

He subsequently arranged Russian citizenship for the girl. Despite international agreements on returning children to their country of habitual residence, the court declined to order her return to France.

Property and vehicles under threat

A bill supported in the State Duma would allow vehicles stolen or illegally exported from unfriendly countries to be registered in Russia.

Supporters say it addresses legal gaps caused by the breakdown in cooperation with Western states; opponents say it would weaken property protections for owners in those countries.

In a separate case, the Supreme Court ordered the Interior Ministry to register a vehicle flagged in an international database at Canada's request, ruling that listing in an international stolen vehicles register is not in itself sufficient grounds to refuse registration in Russia.

Putin signed a decree this autumn under which individuals who cannot prove citizenship of Russia or a friendly state or produce a residency permit are automatically treated as persons from unfriendly countries.

A further decree allows Russian debtors to withhold payment from creditors in unfriendly countries, departing from the standard principle of equal treatment of parties to contracts.

Standard principles of private international law require courts to resolve contracts, custody matters and property disputes on their legal merits, regardless of the nationality or political status of the parties.

Russia’s application of a foreign-policy designation to those areas departs from norms in conventions it has ratified, among them the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, which obligates signatory states to return children removed across borders without consent.

What sounds like science fiction is becoming a concrete research project: the German Aerospace Center (DLR), NASA and Canada's CSA are developing a concept for lunar greenhouses.

How can you grow vegetables in a place that has no life-friendly atmosphere, no fertile soil and no readily available water?

This is precisely what the international Lunar Agriculture Module - Ground Test Demonstrator (LAM-GTD) project (source in German) is about.

The German Aerospace Center (DLR) is working with NASA and the Canadian space agency CSA on concepts for greenhouses on the Moon. They are initially intended to supply astronauts on future long-term missions with fresh food.

A greenhouse as life insurance in space

Temperatures on the Moon fluctuate extremely, its surface is almost airless, water is scarce and cosmic radiation poses a considerable danger. Simply planting crops in lunar soil is not an option. What is needed are controlled cultivation systems that work independently of natural environmental conditions.

The idea is to connect a greenhouse module directly to a simulated living and working area for astronauts. This will allow researchers not only to study plant growth but also to test how the greenhouse and habitat can supply each other.

The planned demonstrator will first be built entirely on Earth. By 2032 at the latest, the three partners want to decide whether and how it will actually be constructed.

NASA in particular has already carried out numerous experiments of this kind on the International Space Station ISS. Among other things, lettuce, Chinese cabbage and chilli peppers have already been grown there.

The next step is to move from small experimental systems on the ISS to significantly larger and more complex cultivation systems that could supply entire crews.

The German partner, DLR, can draw on experience from earlier projects, in particular the EDEN ISS greenhouse, which was operated in Antarctica for several years.

From 2018 to 2023, researchers operated a specially developed greenhouse in Antarctica, only a few hundred metres from the German research station Neumayer III. Under extreme conditions, they grew fresh vegetables there without soil and without natural sunlight. LED lamps, artificial nutrient solutions and a sophisticated irrigation system made it possible to harvest lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, radishes and even strawberries. In total, they produced around one tonne of fresh vegetables.

A project of international cooperation

Antarctica is not the Moon, but it does offer an important similarity: supplies are difficult, environmental conditions are demanding and mistakes can quickly become a problem.

The fact that Germany, the United States and Canada are working together on LAM-GTD is no coincidence. DLR contributes its knowledge from space research and previous greenhouse projects. NASA is working on the conditions for future lunar missions and a long-term human presence on the Moon. The Canadian space agency CSA adds its expertise in space research and in technologies for crewed missions to the collaboration.

One small step for lettuce, one giant leap for humankind

The research is not only of interest to astronauts, because there are also places on Earth where growing food is difficult, such as dry desert regions or areas with limited water resources.

Technologies that allow plants to grow with as little water, energy and space as possible could also help there. Controlled greenhouses could also help produce food more precisely and with less use of plant protection products.

Looking beyond Earth could therefore generate knowledge that helps us find new ways of doing things on our own planet.

What sounds like science fiction is becoming a concrete research project: the German Aerospace Center (DLR), together with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency CSA, is developing a concept for greenhouses on the Moon.

How can vegetables be grown in a place with no habitable atmosphere, no fertile soil and no freely available water?

This is exactly what the international Project Lunar Agriculture Module - Ground Test Demonstrator (LAM-GTD) (source in German) is about.

The German Aerospace Center (DLR) is working together with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency CSA on concepts for greenhouses on the Moon. These are initially intended to supply astronauts on future long-term missions with fresh food.

A greenhouse as life insurance in space

Temperatures on the Moon fluctuate extremely, its surface is almost airless, water is scarce and cosmic radiation poses a considerable danger. Simply putting plants into lunar soil is not an option. Controlled cultivation systems are needed that can operate independently of natural environmental conditions.

The idea is that a greenhouse module will be directly connected to a simulated living and working area for astronauts. This would allow researchers not only to study plant growth, but also to test how the greenhouse and habitat can supply each other.

The planned demonstrator is to be built entirely on Earth to begin with. By 2032 at the latest the three partners want to decide whether and how it will actually be constructed.

NASA in particular has already carried out numerous experiments of this kind on the International Space Station ISS. Among other things, lettuce, Chinese cabbage and chilli peppers have been grown there.

The next step now moves on from small experimental setups on the ISS to much larger and more complex cultivation systems that could supply entire crews.

The German partner, DLR, can draw on experience from earlier projects, in particular the EDEN ISS greenhouse, which was operated in Antarctica for several years.

From 2018 to 2023 researchers ran a specially designed greenhouse in Antarctica, just a few hundred metres from the German research station Neumayer III. Under extreme conditions they grew fresh vegetables there without soil and without natural sunlight. LED lamps, artificial nutrient solutions and a sophisticated irrigation system made it possible to harvest lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, radishes and even strawberries. In total, around one tonne of fresh vegetables was produced.

A project built on international cooperation

Antarctica is not the Moon, but it offers an important similarity: supplies are difficult, environmental conditions are demanding and mistakes can quickly become a problem.

It is no coincidence that Germany, the United States and Canada are working together on LAM-GTD. DLR contributes its expertise from space research and previous greenhouse projects. NASA is working on the foundations for future lunar missions and a long-term human presence on the Moon. The Canadian Space Agency CSA adds its experience in space research and in technologies for crewed missions.

A small step for lettuce, a giant leap for humanity

The research is not only of interest to astronauts, because there are also places on Earth where growing food is difficult, such as arid desert regions or areas with limited water resources.

Technologies that can supply plants with as little water, energy and space as possible could also help in these regions. Controlled greenhouses could also contribute to producing food more precisely and with less use of pesticides.

Looking beyond Earth could therefore yield knowledge that helps us find new ways of growing food on our own planet.

Artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape, creating opportunities for both better defence and attack, according to the latest report from ENISA.

Europe has been hit with numerous cyber incidents in recent months, raising widespread concern, not just from governments but from the public too, about how vulnerable society is to cyber-attack and how prepared the continent is to deal with future cyber threats.

“When we look at the threats landscape, the picture is not so rosy,” said ENISA Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar at a press conference today.

Recent incidents range from the PHP vulnerability, which prompted numerous EU governments to take down their websites to prevent exploitation by hackers, to the wave of cyber-attacks on fridges at supermarkets and blood banks in France and eight other countries resulting from vulnerabilities in out-of-date software.

Cyber threats are evolving and becoming more visible, thanks in part to AI, and now require organisations to keep pace with the latest artificial intelligence model advancements in a kind of cyber arms race.

“Recent developments not only in frontier AI models but also cyber incidents in refrigeration systems across the EU underline the operational gaps and the need for timely information sharing and coordination,” said Lepassaar.

ENISA also calls AI a “force multiplier”, expanding and accelerating the ability of both hackers and the companies defending themselves to spot vulnerabilities more quickly.

“Data synthesised by researchers shows that the time between discovery and weaponisation is approaching zero,” says the report, suggesting that soon companies may have no time at all to protect themselves from vulnerabilities once systems are launched.

At the same time, the report says frontier AI is having a tremendous impact on vulnerability management by narrowing response and patch timings, meaning that companies can use AI to proactively check for vulnerabilities and address them before they are exploited by hackers.

Beyond AI being used as a tool by hackers to scout for vulnerabilities at scale, the report also highlights that AI will sharpen hackers’ existing weapons.

For example, AI tools allow attackers to carry out ever more convincing phishing operations using deepfake videos, audio and messages to trick people and “feed wrong data into systems to disrupt corporate operations”.

Factors driving cyber threats

The report found that 57.3% of cyber incidents in 2025 were ideologically driven by geopolitical events such as Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East, although most had limited impact.

Meanwhile, 29.3% of incidents were financially motivated, with ransomware remaining the most impactful incident type on businesses. The report warns that the ease with which criminals are able to share ransomware and other malware tools is “fuelling a professional criminal ecosystem”.

ENISA also notes that attacks resembling those orchestrated by state actors have been seen targeting European countries to conduct cyberespionage campaigns, collect intelligence and steal intellectual property.

Hacktivists, says ENISA, dominate reporting in terms of the volume of attacks, with most attacks being low-impact distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) operations.

Europe’s response

The EU has put in place myriad cyber rules to tighten up the bloc’s cybersecurity, but ENISA argues more can be done, and it’s hard to disagree given the recent wave of cyber incidents.

The pillar of Europe’s cybersecurity rules is the NIS2 Directive, which obliges all economic sectors to put in place digital safeguards to protect critical infrastructure. However, despite entering into application in October 2024, it hasn’t been transposed into law in all EU member states.

The recent attack on fridges in nine EU countries revealed that there are gaps in some economic sectors’ cybersecurity and in how they determine what is critical infrastructure.

Cybersecurity experts have said many businesses such as supermarkets view cybersecurity through a traditional lens, focusing on financial cybersecurity and leaving connected infrastructure in the hands of maintenance teams with different budgets and priorities.

There’s also the Cyber Resilience Act, which was adopted in 2024 and will be fully applicable in December 2027. It introduces reporting obligations through a single portal to speed up information sharing and coordination.

The Cyber Solidarity Act, which entered into force in February last year, strengthened the EU’s ability to detect, prepare for and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents, says ENISA, through the creation of the European Cybersecurity Alert System, the Cybersecurity Emergency Mechanism and the EU Cybersecurity Reserve.

Europe’s response needs more AI experts

While Europe’s regulatory framework for cybersecurity is extremely busy, manning the defences is a glaring issue, says ENISA.

The report finds that across all sectors, organisations are struggling to attract and retain cybersecurity talent. It cites a 2025 NIS Investment study which found that 45% of organisations surveyed faced difficulties in finding professionals with the requisite cybersecurity skills.

The report warns that this could create a cybersecurity skills gap, giving wealthier organisations the advantage when competing for what is currently a limited pool of talent.

ENISA calls on member states to address the skills shortage by expanding activities and amplifying EU programmes in the cybersecurity field.

Rays are often accidentally caught in fishing nets, which can cause females to expel their eggs. This Portuguese project gives pups a second chance.

Rare and vulnerable rays in Greece's Thermaic Gulf are being given a greater chance of survival through a new marine biodiversity protection initiative.

A Euronews camera captured the first movements of a newborn Kalkanovatos ray just a few minutes after it hatched in a specially designed aquarium in Halkidiki.

Its egg, together with four others, had been found in fishermen's nets and transferred to a specially designed aquarium. There, the eggs were kept under controlled conditions, with a specialised scientific team monitoring their development up to the moment of hatching and beyond. The initiative is part of the Thermaikos Biodiversity Project, a programme to protect biodiversity in the northern Aegean.

This specific action seeks to address 'by-catch', when fishing operations haul in unintended marine life. When a female ray is accidentally caught in the nets, the stress may cause it to expel its eggs, which often end up in the sea without any chance of completing their development.

Newborn rays are monitored and then returned to the wild

In the specially designed aquarium, located within the facilities of the Sani hotel on the Kassandra peninsula, special care is taken to replicate the environmental conditions of the surrounding sea. The aim is to ensure the appropriate temperatures and conditions first for hatching and then for the survival of the newborn rays.

As João Bernardo, the scientific coordinator of the Thermaikos Biodiversity Project, explains, the programme gives a second chance to eggs collected from fishermen's nets. After hatching, the young rays are closely monitored, in cooperation with the Lamna Institute in Valencia, for scientific purposes. They are then prepared for their return to the wild.

A few days later, with the help of divers from the environmental organisation iSea, which works to protect aquatic ecosystems and under whose umbrella the Thermaikos Biodiversity Project has been developed, the newborn rays are released into the sea.

They are returned at a specific depth, where the temperature and water quality are close to the conditions they were used to during their stay in the aquarium.

For the young rays, returning to the Thermaic Gulf marks the start of a new journey. Their birth may be the first important step, but survival in the sea remains a difficult process. Having overcome the first obstacle, which in their case was their very birth – something that was far from guaranteed – they now have to survive in their natural environment and help maintain future generations of their species.

Why do rays need protection?

Rays are among the most threatened groups of fish worldwide, and their conservation is directly linked to the balance and health of marine ecosystems. Almost half of ray species in Greece are at risk of extinction according to the Greek Red List, with by-catch being their main threat.

So far, using the process described, two small Kalkanovatos rays have hatched in 2026 and have already been released into their natural environment in the Halkidiki area, while other eggs are under observation and are expected to hatch in the near future.

The restoration of threatened ray species is one of the actions of the Thermaikos Biodiversity Project. The programme started five years ago with the initial aim of systematically monitoring the dolphins of the Thermaic Gulf. The programme has since expanded its scope, linking scientific research with the protection of marine life and efforts to tackle the impacts of human activity.

Slovakia's Robert Fico accused the German chancellor of "blackmail" as four EU countries resisted his demand to link approval of the bloc's next long-term budget to fresh financial support for Ukraine.

The leaders of Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have pushed back against German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's ultimatum to make approval of the EU's next long-term budget conditional on fresh financial support for Ukraine.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico denounced the move as a "textbook case of blackmail" and threatened to wield his veto.

"We have an equal say in this matter," Fico said on Tuesday as he welcomed his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, in Bratislava.

"Just as Mr Merz talks about using his veto, I can say exactly the same. We have the same veto power as the German federal chancellor."

Babiš quipped that Merz "probably doesn't realise" that the proposed EU budget already earmarks €100 billion for Ukraine. However, those funds will not become available until 2028, while Kyiv faces a €70 billion shortfall next year.

"Today will not be business as usual – not by a long shot. Today, we must respond to blackmail," Fico said, expressing his displeasure.

"What the federal chancellor is doing is a textbook case of blackmail, and I reject it. We are a sovereign country. We are the Slovak Republic. We have our own views."

Merz upped the ante in a letter to European Council President António Costa, declaring that fresh aid for Ukraine was an "essential prerequisite" for approving the next EU budget. The move effectively links two highly contentious issues, both of which require unanimity.

Brussels has promised to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's €70 billion gap, roughly €45 billion, through a yet-to-be-defined instrument. Given the massive scale of the needs, a new round of joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunner option.

The new funding would come on top of an existing €90 billion support loan, from which Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary secured exemptions.

"Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support," Merz wrote.

Merz received Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar in Berlin on Tuesday, just a day after the letter became public.

At the end of the bilateral meeting, Magyar made clear he opposed linking the EU budget with Ukraine aid, arguing the two issues are intrinsically distinct.

"It is possible, obviously, that it has to do a lot with politics. I do not consider this to be blackmail. So I do not use any such words, because everything is connected to everything in today's world," he said, referring to Fico's earlier comments.

"But I think that this does not necessarily have a good message."

Magyar said Hungary could not commit to fresh debt at the European level because it is already struggling to rein in its soaring public deficit.

"In this regard, this is obviously unacceptable for us for domestic political reasons, but we will negotiate in Berlin, Dublin and Brussels," he said.

"We will find a solution for the EU budget. I am sure of it."

Speaking in Varna, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev also pointed to high deficit levels as a reason to exempt his country from future credit lines to Ukraine. Radev said his country will continue support through other means, such as energy flows.

"Bulgaria is in no way blocking the decisions at the Council level that are taken in unity for everyone to support (Ukraine) as they can," Radev said.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria all belong to the "Friends of Cohesion", a group of 17 countries that wants to protect cohesion and agricultural funds in the next long-term EU budget. This has put them on a collision course with the "frugals", who demand across-the-board reductions.

The "frugals" include some of the largest donors to Ukraine, such as Germany, and resent how Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria are trying to opt out of support to Ukraine while, at the same time, demanding cohesion funds.

Speaking alongside Magyar in Berlin, Merz insisted that support for Ukraine must be shared more fairly.

"It's not a good option to continue down this path. Ukraine policy should be fully included in the European Union budget," he said.

"At least four countries think differently, but it is definitely important to talk about this."

From higher-yield orchards to modern irrigation and digital farming, Uzbekistan is changing how its farms operate. Business Line examines the investment and support behind these developments, and the challenge of increasing exports while securing domestic food supplies.

Agriculture remains an important part of Uzbekistan's economy, but the sector faces growing pressure to increase productivity while managing limited land and water resources.

The government is introducing new farming methods, irrigation systems and digital technologies to improve crop yields and support domestic food production, while helping producers compete in international markets.

According to Agriculture Minister Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov, Uzbekistan produces around 26 million tonnes of fruit and vegetables annually, with agricultural products reaching 92 international markets.

The government aims to increase food exports to $10bn (€8.6bn) by 2030. It has also designated 2026–2030 as a priority period for food security, focusing on domestic production and reducing dependence on certain imports.

Higher yields and modern fruit production

One of the government's priorities is to increase agricultural output without relying solely on expanding cultivated land.

"We are paying particular attention to increasing yields through scientific research and the introduction of new innovations. This is important, first and foremost, from the perspective of food security," said Shamshod Ergashev, Head of the Secretariat of the Minister of Agriculture.

In 2025, cotton was grown on approximately 875,600 hectares, compared with more than one million hectares in previous years. Despite the reduction, production reached nearly four million tonnes, according to Ergashev.

He also said Uzbekistan harvested 10 million tonnes of grain in 2026, partly due to improved seed treatment and planting methods.

Uzbekistan has around 572,600 hectares of orchards and vineyards, with plans to develop 172,000 hectares of modern, high-yield orchards between 2026 and 2028.

"Traditional orchards used to produce seven to ten tonnes of fruit per hectare. Now, with trees grown on dwarf and semi-dwarf rootstocks, we are achieving 30 to 35 tonnes, and in some cases even 50 to 60 tonnes," said Abror Jo'rayev, Head of the Republican Horticulture Development Department.

At a 138-hectare orchard growing apples, pears, plums, peaches and apricots, modern cultivation methods are already being used.

A representative of the enterprise, Qahramon Ilhombekov, said the farm produces an average of 35 tonnes of apples per hectare.

"We can produce 50 tonnes, but that puts too much pressure on the trees. At 30 to 35 tonnes, we get fruit with the size, colour and quality we want," he explained.

To encourage investment, the government has introduced preferential loans of up to 120 million soums (€8,873) per hectare for orchard development, with a seven-year loan term, including a three-year grace period.

Farmers can also receive maintenance subsidies of five million soums (€370) per hectare annually for three years, alongside support for irrigation equipment and planting materials.

Irrigation investment and agricultural technology

Water scarcity remains a major challenge for Uzbekistan's agricultural sector, making irrigation efficiency an investment priority.

According to the World Bank, agriculture accounts for around 90% of Uzbekistan's water consumption. In May 2025, the bank approved a $200m (€172m) project to modernise irrigation infrastructure across five regions.

The project aims to reduce annual water losses by approximately 540 million cubic metres and improve irrigation services across 232,000 hectares of agricultural land.

At farm level, drip irrigation is helping farmers manage water consumption and fertiliser application more precisely.

"Water scarcity is becoming an increasing problem. With drip irrigation, water reaches the tree itself rather than the surrounding soil," Jo'rayev explained.

The country received 100 Chinese-made agricultural drones in 2026 through an initiative involving the Ministry of Agriculture and World Bank support.

Half are intended for remote monitoring of farmland, while the others will be used for fertiliser application, pest control and other agricultural operations.

The government is also developing satellite-based crop monitoring, geographic information systems and AI applications for yield forecasting and pest detection.

Meanwhile, digital platforms are being developed to simplify agricultural subsidies and services, with the Agroportal and Agrosubsidy systems intended to reduce administrative procedures.

Climate resilience and financing

Uzbekistan is also seeking investment in agricultural practices that can better withstand environmental pressures.

The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) has been involved in climate-smart agricultural projects, including initiatives in Karakalpakstan.

"Our intervention was mainly about how to scale up climate-smart solutions in agriculture, from pilots to larger investment projects," said Bakhtiyar Radjabov, Senior Officer for Green Growth Policy and Government Liaison at GGGI.

GGGI has supported Uzbek commercial banks in issuing green bonds on the London Stock Exchange to mobilise financing for environmentally focused projects.

Radjabov also highlighted an agrifood investment platform involving the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture, which aims to mobilise around $1.5bn (€1.3bn) for the sector.

He stressed the need for stronger local expertise and the capacity of agricultural businesses to adopt new technologies, particularly as water scarcity, soil salinity and land degradation continue to affect the sector.

Balancing exports and domestic food security

Uzbekistan's agricultural strategy combines plans to increase export revenues with efforts to strengthen domestic food supplies.

The government is encouraging investment in food processing, packaging and higher-value agricultural production to help local producers meet international market requirements.

However, Uzbekistan remains dependent on imports for some essential food products, including vegetable oil and sugar.

"We are introducing new technologies in farming and horticulture, increasing productivity and expanding the export geography of our fruit and vegetables to new countries," Ergashev said.

The longer-term results will depend on whether these investments help farmers improve productivity, manage costs and expand access to markets while responding to water shortages and climate pressures.

Falls pose a significant health risk for older adults, and the likelihood and severity of fall-related injuries increase with age. Yet many people remain unaware of the factors that contribute to falls, including anxiety, hearing loss and mobility problems.

After falling down stairs more than a dozen times, Ben Melancon, a former athlete now in his 70s, became afraid to use them.

“I was scared to death of those stairs,” Melancon said in a press release from The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. His final fall caused an injury that required nine stitches near his left eye.

“That was pretty much the icing on the cake,” Melancon said.

Melancon is one of many older people whose experiences with falling can lead to a lasting fear of losing their balance. But while this fear may lead to avoiding potentially dangerous activities, it can also increase their risk of falling by making them less active and reducing their strength and mobility.

“When you’re not confident, you may avoid activities because you’re afraid you’re going to fall,” said Michelle Easley, a board-certified nurse practitioner at Ohio State Wexner Medical Center’s Fall Prevention Clinic. “That fear of falling is actually one of the biggest risks of falling.”

A new national survey of 1,007 United States adults from The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center found that 63% do not recognise anxiety about falling as a risk. The survey also found that 60% do not recognise hearing loss as a risk, while 74% do not recognise that an urgent need to use the bathroom can increase the chance of falling.

“The number one risk for a fall is a previous fall,” Easley said. “If more people knew about this, we could intervene earlier, get people help and prevent more serious falls.”

Falls across Europe

The problem extends well beyond the United States. Falls are a major public health concern across Europe, contributing to hospital admissions, disability, loss of independence and premature death among older people.

According to a European factsheet published by the European Association for Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion EuroSafe, approximately 35,848 people aged 65 and older were reported to die from falls annually in the EU, based on data from 2010 to 2012. Falls were also identified as the leading cause of injury-related emergency department attendances among older people, accounting for 58% of these visits.

Almost half of fall-related emergency department attendances across Europe result in fractures, while around one in five involve injuries to the head. Beyond the physical injuries, falls can lead to anxiety, fear and increased dependence on family carers or admission to residential care facilities.

The severity of injuries increases with age. The factsheet estimates that 32% of fall-related injuries among people aged 65 to 74 require hospital admission. This rises to 39% among those aged 75 to 84 and 45% among people aged 85 and older.

Addressing the risks

Falls are rarely caused by a single factor. They can result from a combination of physical, behavioural and environmental risks.

These include reduced muscle strength, poor balance, impaired vision or hearing, chronic health conditions and the use of multiple medications. Behavioural factors, such as inadequate footwear and changes in mobility caused by fear of falling, can also contribute.

The home is a particularly important setting for prevention. According to the EuroSafe factsheet, 64% of fall-related injuries occur at home. More than half of injuries occurring inside the home happen in living rooms or bedrooms, followed by bathrooms and stairs.

Outside the home, uneven pavements, slippery surfaces and poorly maintained public spaces can also increase the risk.

Improving strength and balance through physical activity, particularly programmes supervised by physiotherapists, is an important part of prevention.

Melancon attended Ohio State's Fall Prevention Clinic several times a week for four months, working with a physical therapist to improve his strength and balance. He also began exercising at home each morning and wearing athletic shoes that provided better support.

He has not fallen since completing the programme.

“I’m not fearful anymore of steps,” Melancon said. “I can go up and down any steps you want.”

European evidence supports a multi-faceted approach, combining individual risk assessments, medication reviews, tailored exercise programmes and improvements to home and public environments. Studies cited in the EuroSafe factsheet suggest that targeted fall-prevention programmes can reduce injury rates by 20% to 40% among high-risk groups.

Easley recommends checking homes for poor lighting, loose rugs and stairs that may be difficult to use. Bathrooms should also be easy to enter and leave safely, without hazards that could cause a fall.

“Rugs are a huge issue, and they need to be removed or secured,” Easley said. “It’s all about safety, not taking away independence.”

People should also review their medications with their healthcare provider or pharmacist, since some can cause dizziness or balance problems.

Melancon encourages others who fear falling to seek help and stay committed to recovery.

“You can do this,” he said. “If you make a commitment and have dedication, you’re going to do it.”

British mobile phone giant Vodafone on Tuesday posted a huge post-tax loss for its first half, linked primarily to a writedown in Germany, but raised its outlook with total revenue increasing.

The group, which late on Monday said it would axe 2,300 jobs in Germany, booked an impairment there totalling €4.85 billion ($5.45bn) for the six months to end-September.

Vodafone added in an earnings statement that it suffered a net loss of €4.79 billion in its first half.

It had reported a profit after tax of €829 million in the first half of its 2025/26 fiscal year.

"I am very happy about our overall group performance, but Germany is not yet where it needs to be," chief executive Margherita Della Valle said in the release.

Vodafone said its Germany impairment was "primarily driven by adverse changes in interest rates".

The telecoms group had in recent years struggled badly in the country after German legislation stopped housing associations bundling TV contracts with rent.

Offsetting Vodafone's latest writedowns, including €2.2 billion linked to taxation in the UK, was news that total revenue grew 11.4% to €21.9 billion in the first half.

This was in large part thanks to the consolidation of VodafoneThree, following Vodafone's buyout of CK Hutchison's stake in the UK joint venture.

Revenue was boosted also by the integration of Kenya's Safaricom and Telekom Romania.

Looking ahead, Vodafone said it expected adjusted earnings of between €13.2 billion and €13.4 billion for its full year, up from €13bn-€13.3bn.

Vodafone made savings of more than €200 million in its first half as it cut 3,000 staff across Europe.

In July, French tycoon Xavier Niel paid €5.1 billion to become Vodafone's largest shareholder.

Following the update, Vodafone's share price dropped 0.8% after initially rising on London's benchmark FTSE 100 index.

"Niel's presence... is likely to keep the pressure on, with the continuing struggles in Germany the next big hurdle to overcome," said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

Della Valle in 2023 launched a sweeping overhaul of the company, including thousands of job cuts and the sale of its operations in Italy and Spain, as it focused on its core Germany and UK markets.

The EU has pledged €10 million for Bulgaria to bolster search and rescue operations in the Black Sea, which is becoming one of the most dangerous transport routes in the world due to continued drone attacks.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced €10 million in emergency funding for Bulgaria on Tuesday to bolster search and rescue operations in the Black Sea, where drone attacks linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine have made commercial shipping increasingly dangerous.

“Drones sinking commercial ships, setting vessels ablaze, killing civilians. Lives are lost at sea. Navigation is disrupted and the cost of insurance is skyrocketing,” she said.

“The intention of these attacks is clear to spread fear and uncertainty in Europe. We know the playbook and we are building resilience against it. So, you can count on a strong and united European response.”

Von der Leyen made the announcement during a visit to the Nikola Vaptsarov Naval Academy in the Bulgarian coastal city of Varna, a day after visiting Bucharest for talks with Romanian President Nicușor Dan.

Speaking alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, she pledged a stronger European response to threats against shipping in the Black Sea.

Radev, who has advocated closer diplomatic engagement with Russia to end the war, declined to attribute responsibility for the recent attacks while investigations remain underway.

“We would like to receive further data and specific facts as to who the perpetrator is,” he told reporters at the joint press conference. In the past, however, Radev has stated that “logic” suggests that the attacks are due to Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine.

On Monday, von der Leyen began her tour of the EU’s Black Sea countries impacted by recent drone attacks. From Bucharest, she announced a similar €10 million would be provided to Romania to bolster search and rescue operations.

Up to €50 million would be earmarked for the “fast-tracked” development of the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, which would impact both countries, von der Leyen said. Romania’s previous foreign Oana Țoiu said the hub would be located in both Romania and Bulgaria’s main ports, Constanța and Varna, respectively.

The hub sits at the core of the EU’s Black Sea Strategy, published mid-2025. It has been touted as a centre that will coordinate support and boost coast-guard cooperation for the EU countries’ potential dangers and incoming threats, such as cable-cuts and other incendiary activities.

Von der Leyen promised a “clear timeline for completion” of the project. European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho clarified on Tuesday that Brussels aims to have the hub operational by 2027.

Russia has recently intensified strikes on Ukrainian Black Sea vessels and infrastructure, on which Kyiv relies for the export of around 90% of its agricultural commodities. Attacks on storage facilities within Ukraine have also intensified.

Ukrainian Minister for Agrarian Policy and Food, Taras Vysotskyi,told Euronews in September that there had been “some progress” in ensuring Ukrainian harvests reach the market through the Black Sea through European support, through the development of “solidarity lanes”.

A €232m ($260m) wind power project in western Uzbekistan is nearing completion, combining electricity generation with large-scale battery storage in what the Asian Development Bank (ADB) describes as a first for Central Asia.

At Nukus 2, 25 of the 26 wind turbines are already generating electricity, while the battery system is undergoing commissioning. The technology is designed to address a challenge increasingly facing electricity networks around the world, including in Europe: how to balance supply and demand as wind and solar power expand.

The facility, located in Karakalpakstan, an autonomous republic in northwestern Uzbekistan, is being developed by Saudi energy company ACWA. It combines a 200-megawatt wind farm with a battery system capable of storing 100 megawatt-hours of electricity.

According to project director Sardorbek Mahmudov, once fully operational, the facility could meet the electricity needs of more than 300,000 people.

An update published on 26 October put construction progress at 94.2%.

"The wind farm began generating electricity in August," Mahmudov said. He explained that commissioning the batteries involves additional safety and fire-protection requirements, with testing being carried out in stages.

From generation to storage

Wind and solar electricity generation fluctuates with weather conditions, while consumer demand follows a different pattern.

Battery storage offers one way to manage that difference. Electricity can be stored when it is available and released when needed, helping grid operators balance supply and demand and reducing the risk of interruptions.

At Nukus 2, the batteries are intended to provide short-term support when wind generation falls or demand increases.

Asked how long the system could supply electricity, Mahmudov estimated "three to four hours", depending on demand. The actual duration depends on how much power is drawn from the batteries.

The project also includes a new 44-kilometre transmission line and upgrades to existing electrical infrastructure, connecting the facility to Uzbekistan's national grid.

The growing importance of storage extends well beyond Central Asia.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), 108 gigawatts of new battery storage capacity was installed worldwide in 2025, an increase of 40% compared with the previous year.

Europe is experiencing a similar shift. Although total new battery installations across all categories declined slightly, additions of large-scale battery storage more than doubled in 2025, reaching approximately 4.6 gigawatts.

International investment and long-term financing

The project is being implemented through ACWA Beruniy Wind, a local subsidiary of the Saudi developer.

In September 2025, ADB and a fund it administers signed a loan package worth approximately €46mn ($51mn).

Other lenders include the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Dutch development bank FMO, Standard Chartered and Saudi EXIM. AIIB has separately approved approximately €67mn ($75mn) in financing for the project.

ADB also provided a government-backed credit guarantee intended to reduce financial risks and encourage competition during the bidding process.

The investment operates under a 25-year power purchase agreement signed in March 2024 following a competitive tender. Under the agreement, Uzbekistan's national grid operator will purchase electricity generated by the wind farm.

The long-term arrangement provides a commercial framework for the project, combining private investment with an agreed buyer for its electricity.

Abdulatif Matkarimov, an ADB portfolio manager, said the bank had been supporting Uzbekistan's renewable energy development since an earlier project in Navoi.

"In total, there are around ten projects in this sector," he said, referring to wind and solar generation.

Local employment and community impact

Construction has also created employment opportunities in Karakalpakstan.

According to Mahmudov, between 750 and 800 people worked on the project during construction, including more than 400 local workers and specialists.

"Local specialists are now taking on management roles in projects of this scale," he said.

Tarana Jafarova, the project's social manager, said recruitment from nearby communities was intended to support local incomes and livelihoods. She also described procedures for addressing complaints and compensating people affected by construction.

Environmental assessments have identified potential impacts on land use and wildlife, requiring mitigation and monitoring measures.

Once fully operational, the wind farm is expected to generate nearly 728,000 megawatt-hours of electricity annually, according to ADB.

The developer aims to complete commissioning of the battery system by the end of November 2026, bringing the entire facility into full operation.

Two storms, Charles and Bruna, are expected to bring a sharp turn in the weather to Portugal, hitting the Atlantic archipelago of Madeira from late on Tuesday and the mainland throughout Wednesday.

The Portuguese government has issued a warning on social media. “Only go out if it is really necessary”, it said, “especially during peaks of rain and wind”. Anyone who has to drive should do so “with maximum caution”.

The authorities also advised people to keep torches or another source of light and charged devices such as power banks close at hand.

Portugal’s weather service, the Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera (source in Portuguese) (IPMA), has issued orange warnings for rain, wind and rough seas in several mainland districts. They are Lisbon, Évora, Faro, Setúbal, Santarém, Leiria, Beja and Castelo Branco.

IPMA said the effects of Charles were expected to be felt on the mainland from late Tuesday morning, with rainfall “at times heavy over most of the territory”. Gusts could reach 120 km/h and waves up to six metres.

Red warning in Madeira

In Madeira, a red warning, the highest level, is in force for the mountains and the south coast from 9pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday. It will then drop to orange until 9am.

Madeira’s north coast is under an orange warning from 9pm to 9am, and the neighbouring island of Porto Santo is under a yellow warning for the same period.

IPMA is forecasting rain or showers from Tuesday afternoon, at times heavy and persistent, and possibly thunderstorms. Winds could reach 130 km/h on high ground, and waves on the south coast could reach 4.5 metres.

The government warned of the risk of flooding, landslides, collapsing structures, falling trees and objects, and accidents on the coast. Power and communications could be cut at times.

How to prepare

The government is urging people to clear drains, gutters and channels of water and debris so they do not get blocked, and to remove anything else that could stop water flowing away.

People should stay away from rivers, streams and places that have flooded before. The government warns that “water hides holes and open manholes and can sweep away people and cars”.

Beaches, cliffs, breakwaters, piers, riverbanks and anywhere else water could overflow are also dangerous.

Drivers are advised not to park in flood-prone areas, in underground car parks or under trees. Scaffolding and other structures that could fall should be properly secured.

The government also warned that drainage systems will not be able to cope with the amount of rain expected, so several places, including towns and cities, will flood.

130 incidents in Lisbon overnight

Lisbon’s fire brigade, the Regimento de Sapadores Bombeiros (RSBL), dealt with 130 weather-related incidents between midnight and 6am on Tuesday. Most involved flooding in homes and public spaces, and none caused significant damage.

“We had some situations with roads closed in the area of the Segunda Circular, in Campo Grande, and in Prior Velho and Olivais, but these have already been resolved”, a source from the brigade told Portuguese news agency Lusa. Three trees also came down, without harming people or property.

Portugal’s National Authority for Emergency and Civil Protection (ANEPC) was due to give an update on the storm’s effects at a press conference at 8:30am on Tuesday.

Senatorul AUR Ștefan Geamănu a devenit viral pe Facebook şi TikTok cu un discurs în care leagă un proiect de lege privind sănătatea mintală a adolescenților de tratamente hormonale făcute în numele „progresismului” și de un proiect european care nu are, în realitate, nicio legătură cu inițiativa parlamentară. 

Afirmaţie 

„USR și Choice vor să castreze chimic copiii României. Părinții afară din școli (…) Colegii de la USR au depus un proiect de lege prin care un copil de 16 ani poate primi consiliere psihologică fără acordul părinților, fără mamă, fără tată, doar el și specialistul progresist (…) În Comisia de Sănătate, pe cine aduc useriștii să susțină legea? Asociația Choice! Știți cine este Choice? Este proiectul european Choice: Promoting school environments inclusive of diversity based on SOGI, adică educaţie pe orientare sexuală şi identitate de gen în şcolile din România, plătit din bani europeni – o reţea care promovează în şcoli agenda LGBTQ+, care are ca parteneri MozaiQ, ACCEPT, ILG Europe şi care vrea să ne înveţe copiii ce este [sic] homofobia şi transfobia”.

Senatorul AUR Ștefan Geamănu a lansat aceste acuzaţii complet nefondate și nesusținute cu probe într-un discurs susţinut în plenul Parlamentului cu privire la proiectul legislativ L478/2026, iniţiat de parlamentarii USR, care a devenit viral pe reţelele de socializare la finalul lunii septembrie.

Canale

Discursul a fost rostit iniţial în Parlament, iar segmentul de aproape trei minute în care senatorul vorbeşte despre proiect şi îi întreabă retoric pe parlamentarii USR dacă vor să bombardeze “niște copii care nu au trecut nici măcar prin pubertate cu blocante și cu hormoni”, a strâns apoi sute de mii de vizualizări în online, în special pe TikTok şi Facebook.

Pe TikTok, videoclipul a strâns, până la momentul publicării acestui articol, peste 430.000 de vizualizări, 34.000 de reacţii şi 1.700 de comentarii. Acelaşi videoclip, postat şi pe Facebook, a strâns în jur de 30.000 de vizualizări, o mie de reacţii, tot atâtea distribuiri şi câteva zeci de comentarii.

sursa foto: captură de ecran

Alte videoclipuri pe acest subiect postate de senator pe pagina sa de TikTok au strâns câteva sute până la câteva mii de reacţii în zilele care au urmat.

Ce verificăm

Verificăm, în primul rând, dacă proiectul legislativ propus de USR, L478/2026, include “castrarea chimică” a copiilor prin prescrierea de tratamente medicamentoase cum ar fi blocantele de pubertate sau alţi hormoni, după cum insinuează senatorul. De asemenea, verificăm dacă reprezentanţi ai Choice au vreun proiect finanţat de Uniunea Europeană și dacă au susţinut proiectul alături de USR în Comisia de Sănătate a Senatului.

În ceea ce priveşte prima acuzaţie adusă de senator, textul complet al proiectului legislativ propune doar ca adolescenții care au împlinit 16 ani să poată beneficia de evaluare psihologică clinică, consiliere psihologică și psihoterapie fără acordul părinților, inclusiv în cabinetele de consiliere din școli. Accesul la aceste servicii ar fi condiționat de evaluarea capacității cognitive a minorului de către un psiholog autorizat.

Documentul de două pagini nu conține, însă, nicio prevedere legată de administrarea de blocante de pubertate, tratamente hormonale şi nici nu menţionează în vreun fel problema identităţii de gen.

În orice caz, proiectul se referă strict la servicii oferite de psihologi, care nu au competența legală de a prescrie medicamente. Potrivit Ordinului Ministerului Sănătății nr. 1992/2023, serviciile pe care aceștia le pot furniza includ psihologia clinică, consilierea psihologică, psihoterapia și alte intervenții psihologice, nu prescrierea de tratamente medicamentoase.

În România, există și reglementări specifice pentru prescrierea tratamentelor hormonale la copii. De exemplu, conform protocolulului terapeutic din 2022 pentru triptorelină, un medicament utilizat inclusiv pentru blocarea pubertății precoce, stabilește că tratamentul trebuie inițiat de un medic endocrinolog, iar continuarea acestuia poate fi asigurată și de medicul de familie, în condițiile stabilite de specialist.

Pe deasupra, conform proiectului iniţiat de USR, prescrierea de hormoni nu s-ar putea face doar între adolescent şi “specialistul progresist”, iar părinţii nu sunt “daţi afară din şcoli”, pentru că nu le interzice nimeni accesul în instituții, dar mai mult, conform textului de lege, fac excepţie de la regula confidenţialităţii dintre pacient şi psiholog situaţiile în care “specialistul identifică un risc iminent de autovătămare, vătămare a altor persoane, situații de abuz sever sau suspiciunea rezonabilă a unei afectiuni care impune intervenţie medicală”, cazuri în care are obligaţia explicită să-i informeze pe gardienii legali ai minorului şi autorităţile competente, după caz.

Deci nu numai că părinții nu sunt excluși, dar psihologul trebuie să-i contacteze în caz de risc pentru minor. 

În ceea ce privește prezența reprezentanților Choice în Comisia pentru sănătate, senatorul AUR confundă două entități diferite:

  • Asociația Choice din România, înființată în 2015, este o organizație neguvernamentală care promovează psihologia bazată pe dovezi și sănătatea mintală. Preşedintele acesteia, Victor Bohuş, a confirmat pentru Factual că a luat parte la şedinţa comisiei în numele Choice şi al Asociației Psihologilor din România.
  • Proiectul european CHOICE (Promoting School Environments Inclusive of Diversity based on SOGI), care se regăseşte în discursul lui Geamănu, este o inițiativă care urmărește combaterea discriminării și a bullyingului homofob și transfob în școlile din România, Bulgaria, Grecia și Lituania. Printre partenerii proiectului se numără Asociația ACCEPT, care militează pentru drepturile persoanelor LGBT.

În ceea ce priveşte ideea de “educaţie pe orientare sexuală şi identitate de gen în şcolile din România, plătit din bani europeni”, Asociaţia Choice a transmis pentru Context.ro că „nu desfășoară programe sau proiecte în școli, licee sau alte unități de învățământ și nu oferă servicii directe”, dar şi că “singura afiliere europeană…este la Mental Health Europe (MHE), care reunește organizații naționale de sănătate mintală și se preocupa de drepturile și demnitatea persoanelor cu condiții de sănătate mintală și dizabilități psihosociale”.

Verdict

Acuzațiile lui Ștefan Geamănu se bazează pe afirmații false despre conţinutul proiectului L478/2026, care nu face nicio referire la „castrarea chimică” sau la tratamente de schimbare de gen pentru copii, ci prevede posibilitatea ca adolescenții care au împlinit 16 ani să beneficieze de servicii psihologice fără acordul părinților. Textul include și excepții de la confidențialitate în situațiile de risc, iar psihologii nu au competența legală de a prescrie medicamente sau de a stabili diagnostice medicale. 

În plus, fondurile europene invocate de senator sunt asociate unui proiect european CHOICE, dedicat combaterii discriminării în școli, pe care acesta îl confundă cu Asociația Choice din România, organizaţia românească care susţine proiectul.

Montenegro is the first to test the EU's new safeguards, with member states expected to reach a position as early as next week. But contrary to the other negotiating chapters, Podgorica is finding out that the safeguards, including the possibility of suspending voting rights, are non-negotiable.

The EU is discussing stronger safeguards for new member states, including the possibility of suspending voting rights, with Montenegro first in line. But candidate countries face a take-it-or-leave-it deal.

Last month, the European Commission proposed a 15-year probation period for newcomers, designed to allow swift action against those that violate EU values and the principle of sincere cooperation.

The proposal stems from requests by five of the EU’s founding members to draw lessons from the experience of Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, who for years blackmailed the bloc into concessions by wielding his veto over major decisions.

“When I mentioned this for the first time, I said: no new Trojan horses in the European Union. This was still before the elections in Hungary. Today I can say no more Viktor Orbáns,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters presenting the measure.

There is only one catch: candidate countries have no say in these institutional safeguards. They must accept them as they are or walk away from the prospect of EU membership altogether.

For Montenegro, the most advanced candidate, walking away is hardly an option after well over a decade of investing massive administrative capacity, not to mention the political capital of pro-EU forces, in joining the bloc.

Yet changing the terms of membership at the last mile leaves a bitter aftertaste for Montenegrin officials, who are careful not to criticise the measures openly for fear of derailing the process.

“It was always the case. Safeguards were always a bit one-sided,” a senior EU official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

Safeguards per se are not new: they featured in the accession treaties of Croatia, Bulgaria and Romania. But those covered potential breaches of economic, internal market and justice rules.

Now, drawing on Orbán’s experience, Brussels is discussing going as far as suspending a country’s voting rights. Here, too, there is a major difference from the rest of the accession process, procedural as much as political.

Normally, a chapter is opened once the candidate meets the EU’s initial conditions. The candidate then implements the required reforms and meets any interim targets and, once all requirements are fulfilled, the EU agrees to provisionally close the chapter.

This time, Montenegro is not asked to submit a negotiating position, nor to meet any targets beyond accepting what is on the table, making the safeguards effectively non-negotiable.

The Commission is currently preparing EU common positions under Chapters 34 and 35, including draft treaty provisions on institutional safeguards.

Last month, it sent a first draft of the safeguards to be included in Montenegro’s accession treaty to member states for feedback. The Irish presidency of the EU Council is now collecting governments’ views and aims to send a consolidated position at ambassador level next week.

Once EU countries finalise their position, which is more general on safeguards for candidate countries, the Commission is expected to reflect it in Montenegro’s treaty.

In other words, Podgorica’s best chance of influencing the outcome is to lobby member states: once the EU position is set, there will be hardly any way to move it.

Three issues dominate the debate: the measures the safeguard could trigger, such as suspending voting rights for the most serious offences; its duration, which candidate countries consider too long at 15 years; and governance, as the proposed decision-making method would give the Commission significant sway.

Some EU capitals are sympathetic to the candidates’ arguments and want to distinguish between the political demand for stricter safeguards and a legal text that can be enforced.

Italy, a member of the so-called Friends of the Western Balkans, has pushed for respecting the equality of member states and for safeguards that are proportionate and tailor-made for each candidate.

The Netherlands, by contrast, has championed no differentiation between EU hopefuls. But whichever worldview will eventually prevail is fully outside Montenegro’s hands.

Former NATO boss Anders Fogh Rasumussen warned Europe against merely pleading to part of the US-brokered ceasefire talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, saying that securing a seat at the negotiating table comes through strength, not “begging”.

Europe must stop begging for a seat at the table in US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine and instead prove its relevance, former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen told Euronews.

“Europe is already in a weak position. Europe is begging for a place at the table,” he said. “You have to make yourself indispensable by bringing assets to the table, so I hope Europe will now wake up.”

Rasmussen was speaking as Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at ending Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Senior European officials, including representatives from the European Union, NATO, Britain, Germany, Italy and France, will also travel to the United Arab Emirates for separate discussions but will not take part in the main trilateral meeting.

Their presence reflects Europe's determination to have a say in negotiations whose outcome could reshape the continent's security.

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, said last week that a “new European security architecture” would be a focus of the talks. Russian officials have used similar language in calling for a reduced NATO presence in Europe.

“We have seen US President Donald Trump chose Moscow,” Rasmussen said, “and siding with Putin.”

“This is a situation we have to take seriously. The Europeans must wake up. If we don't, we will be sleepwalking into a permanent war on the European continent.”

A 90-minute phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, initiated by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, exposed divisions among Nordic leaders and highlighted Europe's struggle to speak with one voice.

The call prompted criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned the decision to engage Moscow without consulting other European leaders.

"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not coordinated with any of us," Frederiksen said shortly after the call became public.

Rasmussen, who served as Danish prime minister from 2001 to 2009, said it was a “good thing” to talk to Russia but stressed that such initiatives should be coordinated.

“And we should understand that we in Europe cannot be neutral mediators. We will side with the Ukrainians,” he said.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has argued that Eastern European countries must have a voice in potential peace talks, as the region is particularly exposed to the spillover effects of Russia's invasion.

“The last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the east Europeans," he said last week.

Rasmussen led the NATO alliance from 2009 to 2014. Just before his tenure, in 2004, the Baltic nations of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania joined both NATO and the European Union.

Asked whether their security interests should be taken into account in the negotiations, Rasmussen said: “We should have listened to the Eastern Europeans.”

Beyond the peace talks, Rasmussen criticised Washington's delays in approving the delivery of US-made air-defence missiles to Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late October that he had been waiting almost a month for US approval of Patriot and NASAMS missile deliveries.

The delays have raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to repel Russian ballistic missile attacks and other aerial threats, which continue to batter the war-weary capital, Kyiv. Rasmussen described the delay as “damning” for Ukraine's defences.

“I'm so disappointed that the Americans have not delivered what they have promised to deliver. I'm not going to guess about the reasons why, but it just underlines the need for us in Europe to be able to stand on our own feet,” he said.

Asked whether he had ever seen NATO as divided as it is today, amid US troop reductions, Trump's threats to withdraw from the alliance and tensions over Greenland, Rasmussen replied: “Not at all.”

“It was an era where we could trust the American ally,” he said.

“When push comes to shove the Americans will come to the aid of Europe, but we have to be able to stand on our own feet. It's high time that we take decisions in Europe irrespective of who is residing in the White House.”

Tokyo says the new equipment will help Manila monitor shipping routes that are also important to Japan.

Japan agreed on Monday to give the Philippine military a coastal radar system and surveillance drones to help it track ships, in a grant worth 4.3 billion Japanese yen (€24 million).

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro and Japan’s ambassador Katsuro Kitagawa signed the agreement in Manila. The radar will go to the Philippine Navy and the drones to the Air Force.

Japan’s foreign ministry said the equipment would also help protect shipping routes important to Japan, including those through the South China Sea and the Luzon Strait, between the Philippines and Taiwan.

Japan handed over five coastal radar systems to the Philippines in February under a 2023 grant. Tokyo says the new radar will be the first complete defence system it supplies under its Official Security Assistance programme.

Beijing has criticised the programme since its creation, calling it an attempt to build a security network around China under the cover of development aid.

The Philippines and China both claim Scarborough Shoal, where China’s military said it sent ships and aircraft on patrol on 30 October.

In a phone call on 3 November, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Manila to act cautiously over the dispute. Lazaro described their conversation as “frank and constructive” and said both sides wanted to keep talking.

Beijing has separately described Japan’s expanding military role in the South China Sea as destabilising, and has accused Tokyo of using its security partnerships with regional states to advance US strategic interests.

China claims historic rights to resources across much of the South China Sea. In a case brought by the Philippines, an international tribunal ruled in 2016 that those claims had no legal basis where they exceeded the rights granted by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Beijing has rejected the ruling.

Japan and the Philippines are also discussing transferring an Abukuma-class destroyer to the Philippine navy.

Their defence ministers said in October that they wanted the handover to take place as soon as possible after Japan retires the ship, which it expects to do in the coming years. Philippine crews would receive training first.

The EU approved a separate €15 million package in July to help Philippine forces monitor the country’s waters.

Its first grant to the Philippines under the European Peace Facility will fund coastal radar, infrared surveillance equipment and training.

Dunagan was six years old when he voiced the young deer in the classic Disney animated film. He went on to enlist in the Marine Corps and retired as a Major with three Purple Hearts.

Donnie Dunagan, who provided the voice of young Bambi in the 1942 Disney classic before embarking in a career in the military, has died aged 92 of lung cancer.

“We were proud to represent a Marine, beloved by fans around the world for his roles in ‘Bambi’ and ‘Son of Frankenstein,'” his agents Kris Jones and Nery Lemus of CelebWorx told Variety. “While he asked us (in his words) ‘not to be sad due to the great life I lived,’ it would be amiss not to share the impact that Donnie had on people when they met him."

They added: "His love for life was shown through his encouragement. He knew how to inspire and inspired us to be the best we could be. He had an infectious smile, a warmth and charisma that never shook the child-like spirit of his acting youth. He rallied other veterans, loved his fans, and above all else, loved his wife. We will always love you Donnie. You were the best of us.”

Born on 16 August 1934, Dunagan was 3 years old when he won a tap-dancing contest and was spotted by a talent scout in the audience. He made his big-screen debut in Mother Carey’s Chickens (1938), directed by Rowland V. Lee - who then cast him alongisde Boris Karloff as Peter von Frankenstein in Son of Frankenstein (1939). He then starred in Tower of London (1939) alongside Basil Rathbone, Vigil in the Night (1940), and Meet the Chump (1941) before being cast in Bambi.

It was to be his last role, as Dunagan later joined the Marines in 1952 at age 18. He became the youngest drill instructor in their history and served three tours in Vietnam before retiring with the rank of Major in 1977. He was awarded a Bronze Star and three Purple Hearts - the oldest active military decoration in the United States, given to military service members who have been wounded or killed in action while serving.

Dunagan told NPR in 2015 that never disclosed his early career to his comrades,as he didn't want to be referred to as "Major Bambi".

“One of the biggest regrets of my life is that I didn’t have the courage to tell my close personal friends in the Marine Corps that I had been a part of the wonderful work of Mr. Disney,” he confessed.

RIP Donald Dunagan 1934 - 2026

Eleven people have been killed and 48 injured in pile-ups on both carriageways of a motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, the authorities said on Tuesday.

“The toll at this point is 11 dead and 48 injured,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters.

The crashes happened on Tuesday morning near the city of Yambol, on the Trakia motorway linking the capital Sofia with Burgas on the Black Sea. More than 50 cars and heavy vehicles were involved.

Drone footage released by Bulgarian broadcaster Nova shows a huge pile-up in thick fog, with lorries, vans and cars jammed across the carriageway. Fire engines and ambulances are lined up along the road as emergency workers in hi-vis jackets move between the wrecked vehicles. Closer shots, shown after a warning about sensitive footage, show several cars badly crushed between lorries while debris is scattered across the road.

According to the news site Novinite, the two pile-ups happened a few kilometres apart near the Zimnitsa junction, one on the Burgas-bound carriageway and the other heading towards Sofia. The first emergency call came at about 7:10am local time (8.10am CET). Dense fog was the main factor Novinite reported, with one eyewitness putting visibility at about 30 metres.

Todor Mishinev, head of Yambol traffic police, said people were trapped, including in tanker lorries. Rescuers had to cut through metal to free them.

Injured people were taken to hospitals in Yambol and the nearby city of Sliven. Several are in a serious or life-threatening condition.

Ministers dispatched to the scene as motorway stays closed

Radev cancelled his engagements in Varna because of the crashes, just after he had met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Bulgaria Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev sent Lyubomir Nikolov, the ministry’s acting chief secretary, and Deputy Interior Minister Kaloyan Kaloyanov to the scene. Health Minister Katya Ivkova was also travelling to the area and was due to give a press briefing at the Dr Ivan Seliminski Hospital in Sliven, according to Novinite.

The motorway has been closed in both directions between the Zimnitsa and Kabile junctions. Bulgaria’s Road Infrastructure Agency said the closure would last for some time because of the heavy vehicles involved and the investigation.

Bulgaria’s roads are ranked the most dangerous in the EU.
