Around 5,800 people are still living in emergency facilities set up after mass arrivals in the territory at the end of July.

Spanish police on Monday launched a fresh operation to clear a temporary migrant camp in the port of Ceuta, Spain’s exclave on the North African coast, with the aim of shutting the site down. According to local media, the move has led to a rise in the number of Moroccans going home.

Officers from Spain’s National Police returned to the camp before 7am, a day after a first operation there on Sunday. The migrants are being moved to other accommodation provided by the government or to the Centre for the Temporary Stay of Foreigners (CATE) in El Tarajal, where their immigration status is checked.

Those who say they want to go back to Morocco can return voluntarily. Others are being transferred to facilities run by the Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration.

Under the government’s plan, all seven temporary reception facilities set up around the city after the mass arrivals at the end of July will be closed in stages. Together they have about 7,000 places and currently house around 5,800 registered people. The dismantling began on Sunday, when 50 tents belonging to the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (Aecid) were taken down on the port’s west quay.

Using port land for reception facilities had been criticised on security grounds, because the port is considered strategically important. In September, the Interior Ministry temporarily tightened maritime security and raised the port’s alert to level 2. It said the camp had changed the normal operating and protection conditions at the site.

The Unified Police Union (SUP) challenged the decision to set up the camp in court and asked for its opening to be suspended. Spain’s National High Court, the Audiencia Nacional, refused to grant that interim measure.

More than 300 Moroccans return home

The closure of the camp has sped up voluntary departures. Local newspaper El Faro de Ceuta reports that more than 300 Moroccans have gone home in the past two days. They had spent more than three months in Ceuta waiting for their cases to be resolved.

Their decision to return may have been influenced by poor prospects of being allowed to stay in Spain and by the rejection of most asylum applications.

According to the latest official figures, 14,818 migrants have returned to Morocco since an estimated 80,000 arrivals in late July. Of these, 14,180 left voluntarily and 638 were deported.

Elma Saiz, Spain’s migration minister, said 6,113 people had so far been through the screening process. Meanwhile, 3,650 minors remain in the care of Ceuta’s local authorities.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that artificial intelligence should be banned wherever it poses a risk to the mental health of children.

"Just because it's AI doesn't mean it should be the Wild West," Macron said, adding that AI should be banned when it "threatened" children's "mental health or their brain".

This charter, which is "intended to inform national and European legislative debates", will bring together, in particular, US giants OpenAI and Anthropic, Macron's office said.

Companies will accept "the principle of a pre-audit and pre-certification, with a prior review of the models before putting them in children’s hands", Macron said.

"We are going to advance European regulation and push for the Americans, the Canadians, and others to do as we do. We are in the process of creating the beginnings of frontier AI regulation," he added.

Macron said the aim was to create "a framework that takes into account the dangers, which fall into three categories: our children, democratic security, and major national security issues".

Macron also brought together around 50 heads of state and government, representatives of international organisations, companies, researchers, and laboratories to discuss the risks AI poses to collective security in a videoconference.

CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology), cel mai mare producător de baterii și stații pentru mașini electrice la nivel global, anunță că își va extinde activitatea în domeniul schimbului de baterii, care le permite șoferilor să înlocuiască bateriile descărcate cu altele deja încărcate. Compania își propune să dispună de peste 3.000 de stații pentru autoturisme în toată China până la sfârșitul anului.

Producătorul chinez promovează tehnologia cu ioni de sodiu pentru vehicule, ca alternativă la bateriile tradiționale cu ioni de litiu. Concret, spre deosebire de stațiile obișnuite, unde mașinile sunt conectate la priză pentru a-și încărca bateriile, aceste puncte permit înlocuirea rapidă a unui acumulator descărcat cu unul complet încărcat, în doar câteva minute. Deși acestea au fost prezentate ca fiind mai sigure și mai ieftine și că ar performa mai bine la temperaturi foarte scăzute, există îngrijorări legate de cantitatea de energie pe care o pot stoca.  

Robin Zeng, președintele CATL, susține că autonomia bateriilor cu sodiu este suficientă pentru deplasările zilnice în oraș. Extinderea rețelei de stații ar calma îngrijorările șoferilor care vor să călătorească pe distanțe mai mari, a mai afirmat Zeng, precizând că în jur de 200 de orașe chinezești dispun deja de astfel de stații.

Compania a declarat că se așteaptă ca, în acest an, între 10 și 20 de mii de vehicule electrice să ajungă să utilizeze bateriile sale cu ioni de sodiu și consideră aceste baterii o strategie de gestionare a riscurilor menită să o protejeze de fluctuațiile bruște ale prețurilor litiului. 

Bateriile cu sodiu folosesc un material mult mai abundent și mai ușor de procurat decât litiul. Sodiul se găsește inclusiv în sarea obișnuită și în apa de mare, în timp ce producția bateriilor tradiționale depinde de materii prime precum litiul, grafitul și cobaltul, pentru unele dintre acestea China având o poziție dominantă pe piața mondială.

Principalul dezavantaj al bateriilor cu sodiu este densitatea energetică mai mică. Cu alte cuvinte, ele pot stoca mai puțină energie într-un anumit volum sau la aceeași greutate, ceea ce înseamnă că o mașină echipată cu asemenea acumulatori poate parcurge distanțe mai mici între încărcări. În schimb, bateriile cu sodiu au avantaje la temperaturi foarte scăzute sau foarte ridicate, pot fi mai sigure și ar putea deveni mai ieftine decât cele pe bază de litiu.

De altfel, o analiză recentă realizată de Financial Times arată că, deși producătorii occidentali sperau să folosească această tehnologie pentru a recupera terenul pierdut în fața Chinei în industria bateriilor, companiile chineze au ajuns deja mult mai departe în dezvoltarea și producția la scară industrială.

Potrivit datelor companiei de consultanță CRU, capacitatea fabricilor de baterii cu sodiu aflate în funcțiune sau planificate în China depășește 400 GWh, în timp ce în restul lumii este de aproximativ 11 GWh. Așadar, diferența este de peste 36 de ori. Producători precum CATL și BYD beneficiază de investiții consistente și de sprijinul statului chinez, în timp ce mai multe companii europene și americane aflate la început de drum au ajuns să se închidă.

Avantajele bateriilor cu sodiu nu se limitează însă la mașinile electrice. Ele sunt considerate o alternativă promițătoare și pentru stocarea energiei electrice produse de parcurile eoliene și solare, dar și pentru centrele de date, care au nevoie de sisteme de rezervă pentru alimentarea cu energie. În aceste domenii, autonomia redusă nu reprezintă un dezavantaj la fel de important ca în cazul automobilelor. Cu toate acestea, specialiștii nu se așteaptă ca bateriile cu sodiu să înlocuiască în totalitate tehnologia bazată pe litiu, ci mai degrabă să o completeze, fiind utilizate în special acolo unde costul, siguranța și funcționarea la temperaturi extreme sunt mai importante decât autonomia.

Pentru Europa și SUA, explică FT, provocarea este și una strategică – dacă vor continua să cumpere baterii și tehnologie din China sau vor investi suficient pentru a-și construi propriile lanțuri de producție și aprovizionare. Deocamdată, avansul chinez este considerabil, iar unele companii occidentale au început chiar să încheie parteneriate cu producători chinezi pentru a avea acces la această tehnologie.

The 500 million DKK (€67 million) investment in Denmark’s AI supercomputer could help create businesses and jobs and enable public institutions to use AI securely, according to Tuesday’s announcement.

Denmark is pouring another 500 million DKK (€66.9 million) into one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, backed by pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk Foundation, under plans announced on Tuesday.

The funding will support its supercomputer Gefion’s infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation (DCAI), which runs the machine, according to an announcement from the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark.

Further details of how the funding will be used and when the additional capacity will be available have not been revealed.

Denmark launched its supercomputer Gefion in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips. The centre says it is now nearing full capacity.

The new investment adds to the initial 700 million DKK (€93.8 million) in funding from Denmark’s state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Danish foundation behind the maker of weight-loss and diabetes drugs such as Ozempic.

‘New solutions, companies and jobs’

The aim is to turn greater access to computing power into economic growth.

“This gives Danish companies and researchers more computing power to translate good ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs,” said Martin Lidegaard, Denmark’s minister for business and competitiveness, in a statement.

“And it also strengthens our competitiveness, while ensuring that ownership of the technology of the future is not left to others,” he added.

Another aim is to help public institutions and businesses use AI while retaining control over sensitive data.

Netcompany, a Danish technology company that builds and operates public-sector IT systems, including for NHS England, is joining the centre’s investors. It will contribute software to manage access, monitoring and security.

What it means for Europe’s push for greater digital control

The announcement comes as European governments race to gain greater control over the infrastructure used to develop AI and the companies building it.

The United Kingdom invested £225 million (€269 million) in a supercomputer dedicated to AI research in 2023.

Meanwhile, Finland hosts a supercomputer, Large Unified Modern Infrastructure (LUMI), jointly funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost of more than €200 million.

In July, the European Commission launched a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, larger data centres built to train and run advanced AI models, backed by up to €10 billion in European Union and national funding.

“Europe must be able to do much more itself, and Denmark must contribute to European technological independence — not least so that we can regulate and develop technology based on democratic values,” said Christina Egelund, Denmark’s minister for research, education and digitalisation.

Another elephant from a circus in Belgium is expected to arrive at the sanctuary as early as November.

Almost four months ago, Portugal's last circus elephant began a peaceful new life in a new sanctuary. Julie is the first resident of the 400-hectare estate in the southern Alentejo region, the first of this scale in Europe.

"Julie [when she arrived] was shy, it is like anyone who comes to a new place, who does not know anyone and does not know the surroundings," says elephant keeper Johnny Nascimento. "Slowly, about a week later, she began to trust and to decide what she wanted to do outside. There are many trails, so she has been tidying up the house and, in this case, making it her own home."

According to the Pangea sanctuary, Julie was moved to the Alentejo in June after a voluntary agreement with the Victor Hugo Cardinali circus. Since then, she has already put on weight and can now move around as she pleases. One of her favourite pastimes is wallowing in mud pools.

'She owns everything': Julie has free rein of the sanctuary 24/7

"She has been with us for just over three months and has already gained about 100 kilos in that time, which is perfectly normal," explains Ryan Hockley, manager of the Pangea Sanctuary. "Where she was before, she did not really have the opportunity to exercise, she was just in a shed most of the time. Whereas now she has free access 24 hours a day, she can be in the shelter, she can be in any habitat, she literally owns everything, she makes her own choices."

Julie was captured in Africa about 40 years ago. She arrived in Portugal when she was still very young and joined the Cardinali circus in 1988.

In 2018, Portugal banned wild animals from circuses, but the law only came into force in 2024, to give circuses time to adapt and find solutions for where to send the animals.

This is part of the reason behind the sanctuary, to be a new home for elephants in need coming from zoos, circuses and other places. It is estimated that there are more than 600 elephants in captivity across Europe.

"I think it is extremely important that someone has done what we are doing, that someone has created an elephant sanctuary. There are more than 600 elephants in Europe, Asian and African, and a proportion of those elephants are not in ideal conditions," laments the head of the sanctuary.

'I think Portugal is the ideal choice'

The Portuguese region of the Alentejo was chosen for its warm climate, which can recreate conditions similar to those of the African continent. "If we were to choose anywhere in Europe, I think Portugal is the ideal choice, the climate gives me that feeling of being in Africa," says Hockley, drawing parallels between the Alentejo region and the landscapes of Tanzania or Kenya.

From now on, Pangea's goal is to keep expanding so that it can take in more animals in the future, with total capacity to house between 20 and 30 elephants.

"We are certainly the first large-scale elephant sanctuary in Europe, there is a sanctuary in France, but the enclosure they have is not as big as the one we have here, we have an incredible piece of land," says Hockley.

Julie will not be alone for much longer. Another elephant from a circus in Belgium is expected to arrive at the sanctuary as early as November. Kariba, another African female, was also captured in the wild.

She should already have been transported to the sanctuary, but a series of infections prevented her from travelling safely. The animal had to be treated and only once all the conditions are in place will she be transported to Portugal.

For the time being, the sanctuary will remain closed to visitors, "providing Julie and future residents with the space and tranquillity they need to adapt".

Pantelimon” din București, au fost trimise în judecată pentru fapte legate de reducerea intenționată și fără justificare medicală a tratamentului unor pacienți internați la Terapie Intensivă, în scopul grăbirii decesului acestora. Potrivit Parchetului de pe lângă Tribunalul București, în urma acestor intervenții au murit patru pacienți, iar în alte două cazuri medicii au dat indicații pentru moartea unor bolnavi, dar aceștia au supraviețuit.

Concret, procurorii susțin că, în perioada mai 2023 – aprilie 2024, medicii selectau dintre pacienții aflați la Terapie Intensivă persoane despre care considerau, “în mod subiectiv și fără o evaluare medicală obiectivă, că nu mai au șanse de supraviețuire”. Ulterior, interveneau asupra tratamentului pentru a le grăbi moartea, deși aveau obligația profesională și legală să acorde îngrijiri tuturor pacienților, indiferent de gravitatea bolii sau de prognostic.

Una dintre metode consta în reducerea bruscă a dozei de noradrenalină, un medicament administrat pentru menținerea tensiunii arteriale la pacienții aflați în stare gravă. Potrivit anchetatorilor, dozele erau coborâte de la niveluri terapeutice ridicate la valori minime, de regulă 1 ml pe oră, deși medicamentul era esențial pentru menținerea tensiunii arteriale la un nivel compatibil cu viața.

O altă metodă era reducerea cantității de oxigen administrate prin ventilatorul mecanic. Medicii coborau concentrația de oxigen până la 21%, adică nivelul existent în aerul atmosferic. În cazul pacienților care aveau nevoie de concentrații mai mari pentru a putea respira, această intervenție putea provoca lipsa de oxigen în organism și, în cele din urmă, decesul.

Procurorii mai spun că, în unele cazuri, medicii nu intervenau pentru resuscitarea pacienților atunci când aceștia intrau în stop cardio-respirator, deși aveau obligația să încerce să le salveze viața.

Anchetatorii susțin că medicii încercau să ascundă intervențiile prin falsificarea documentelor medicale. În foile de observație erau trecute valori ale dozelor de noradrenalină și ale altor parametri care nu corespundeau tratamentului administrat în realitate, ci indicau valorile inițiale sau pe cele care ar fi trebuit să fie administrate.

Procurorii descriu și o practică numită de personalul medical “nora pentru vizită”. Aceasta presupunea creșterea temporară a dozei de noradrenalină la un nivel aparent normal, doar pe durata vizitelor aparținătorilor, astfel încât aceștia să nu observe că tratamentul fusese redus sau întrerupt. După plecarea rudelor, doza era din nou coborâtă la valori minime.

Potrivit rechizitoriului, patru pacienți au murit în urma acestor acțiuni. Într-un al cincilea caz, un medic a încercat să provoace moartea unui pacient, însă fără a reuși, iar într-un al șaselea a dat indicații pentru reducerea dozei de noradrenalină, dar măsura n-a mai fost pusă în aplicare.

Unul dintre medicii trimiși în judecată este acuzat de patru infracțiuni de omor calificat, precum și de instigare la fals intelectual. Decesele vizate sunt cele ale unei paciente din mai 2023, a doi pacienți din 4 aprilie 2024 și al unei alte paciente din 7 aprilie 2024. O a doua doctoriță este acuzată de două infracțiuni de omor calificat, pentru fapte comise împreună cu prima inculpată, în 4 aprilie 2024, precum și de instigare la fals intelectual. Un al treilea medic este acuzat de tentativă de omor calificat, pentru o faptă din 13 aprilie 2023. O a patra doctoriță este acuzată că a încercat să determine o asistentă să comită infracțiunea de omor calificat. "We are calling on everyone who supports the legitimate demands of young people, but also those of workers, to be out on the streets," said Éloïse Lefebvre-Milon, co-leader of the Union étudiante student union, after leaving the talks.

Moscow demands that Ukraine recognise Russian control over Crimea and the four regions it claims to have illegally annexed - Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson - and withdraw its forces from all four regions, including areas Russia has never occupied. Kyiv rejects these demands.

The US official offered no details of the reported flexibility, but cautioned that territorial disputes could not be resolved without agreement on post-war security arrangements.

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said.

Ahead of the talks, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would propose steps to reduce hostilities in Abu Dhabi and seek agreement on how to arrange a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, Russia and the US.

"At the meetings in Abu Dhabi, our team will propose de-escalatory steps, and there must be an understanding of how to arrange a trilateral meeting at the leaders’ level to bring this war to an end fairly and for real," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Abu Dhabi talks begin with European consultations

The negotiations opened on Tuesday with a meeting between Ukrainian, American and European representatives, ahead of the first trilateral talks involving Kyiv, Moscow and Washington since February.

Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said representatives from the UK, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission attended the initial meeting, alongside US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

"We will align our positions and coordinate steps ahead of the next stage of negotiations," Umerov said, referring to the subsequent trilateral format with Russia.

He identified Ukraine's priorities as ending hostilities, securing post-war security guarantees, economic recovery and humanitarian measures.

Post-war security proposals

European leaders have pressed for a greater role in the US-led diplomatic process, particularly as Washington considers arrangements that could reshape the continent's security.

"In order to end the war, you need to have Europe at the table," a senior US official reportedly said ahead of the talks.

According to US media reports, Washington and Moscow have discussed possible security guarantees for Ukraine resembling NATO's Article 4 and Article 5 provisions, which cover consultations over security threats and collective defence respectively.

The official also reportedly raised the possibility of reviving the NATO-Russia Council, suspended since 2022, and introducing a sanctions "snapback" mechanism that would allow restrictions on Moscow to be reinstated if Russia violated a ceasefire.

Meanwhile, Russia's attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure continue. In his evening address on Monday, Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was seeking to divide Ukraine along the Dnipro River by targeting bridges and the power grid.

"Russia is trying to divide Ukraine along the Dnipro River and make life as difficult as possible for people – for our cities and villages," he said.

Despite renewed diplomatic efforts, Washington has cautioned against expectations of an immediate breakthrough.

US envoy Jared Kushner said the talks could help "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations", describing the conflict as "extraordinarily difficult and complicated".

The EPSO generalist exam started on November 9, but almost half of the applicants come from one single country, Italy. This clashes with the Commission's own hiring rules, which favour 'underrepresented countries' to address geographical staff imbalances.

The European Union's 2026 EPSO competition attracted 174.727 candidates competing for 1.490 available reserve list spots. But 79.343, almost half of them, are Italian.

This creates a problem for EU institutions, which face chronic representation imbalances as countries like Germany and France fail to reach the desired staffing levels. In 2025, the Commission introduced new hiring guidelines for teams to prioritise candidates from a list of 15 'underrepresented' countries. These rules apply to applicants who already passed the EPSO exam, at the interview stage.

This raises the possibility that Italians could occupy a substantial share of the 1.490 reserve-list places, complicating efforts to improve geographical representation. Olivier Salles, Director of EPSO (European Personnel Selection Office), told Euronews that past competitions did show a link between nationalities and success.

"Previous competitions suggest that the geographical distribution of successful candidates broadly follows the distribution of applicants," Salles said. "However, some variations can occur, especially if drop-out rates affect different groups differently."

He still cautioned that "it is too early to predict the geographical spread of successful candidates in this competition."

15 'underrepresented' nations

Italy's applicants far exceed Spain (13.789), Germany (11.699) and France (10.939). In fact, Italy alone has more applicants than those three countries combined.

Countries like the Netherlands (2.729), Denmark (987) and Luxembourg (630) have attracted comparatively few candidates. This imbalance matters because the Commission is already struggling to attract staff from Northern and Western Europe. Germany currently sits at just 64% of its targeted staffing level, and France at 73%.

The Commission's own legal framework, under Article 27 of EU Staff Regulations, defines as a "significant imbalance" any staff presence that falls below 80% of its rate (a target based on a country's European Parliament seats and population).

The 15 countries that do not currently reach their staff rate are Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Cyprus, Ireland, Luxembourg, Poland, Slovakia, Lithuania, and Latvia.

Italy has around 1.848 administrators working in the Commission, compared with 1.571 from France, 1.370 from Germany and just 380 from the Netherlands. Denmark has only 191, while Sweden has 264. However, numbers alone don't determine whether a country is underrepresented, since larger countries are expected to contribute more staff.

Germany, for example, has the EU's largest population but relatively few Commission officials for its size. Belgium, meanwhile, is heavily overrepresented, partly because Brussels hosts most of the Commission's workforce.

The Commission is also concerned that an upcoming wave of retirements could worsen geographical imbalances. Some countries are expected to lose a big share of their existing officials, with Germany alone projected to lose around 16% of its current staff to retirement. Without enough new recruits from these countries, their representation could fall further.

The geographical imbalance action plan

To fix this, the Commission developed Joint Action Plans with the 15 member states in 2023, followed by stronger recruitment rules adopted on 6 November 2025.

The plan focuses particularly on younger and early-career officials, in grades AD5 to AD8, who form the future pool of senior EU administrators.

The first measures included recruitment campaigns, university outreach and exam preparation support. But a 2024 review found that these efforts hadn't achieved much. So, in 2025, the Commission introduced stricter hiring rules that require hiring managers to invite at least one qualified candidate from an underrepresented country to final interviews and allow them to favour these candidates when qualifications are equal.

The rules also introduce recruitment targets, although the Commission insists that jobs cannot be reserved for specific nationalities and that all candidates must meet the same standards.

This is where the 2026 EPSO competition creates a potential problem. Italy alone accounts for 45.4% of applicants, despite not being among the 15 underrepresented countries. If Italian candidates pass the examinations in similarly large proportions, they could dominate the reserve list from which EU institutions recruit.

Meanwhile, countries like Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands have considerably smaller applicant pools. Even with preferential interview measures, the Commission cannot recruit candidates from these countries unless enough make it through the examinations.

Spain has already challenged the legality of these measures, arguing that they risk discriminating against candidates from other member states, and France and Belgium supported its case.

Crucially, the rules do not change how candidates are scored in the EPSO examination, which remains merit-based. They apply later, as institutions select candidates from the reserve list for interviews. The Commission also maintains that it reserves no jobs for specific nationalities. Salles added that "available data does not establish significant differences in pass rates between nationalities".

The 2026 EPSO exam

Several factors explain the unprecedented number of applications for the 2026 EPSO competition, including the 7-year-gap since the last generalist competition, the introduction of remote testing, and broader eligibility criteria.

"Since 2019, EPSO has seen a steady increase in applications across all competitions, so the high number of applicants for the AD5 competition is part of a broader trend," Salles said.

He pointed to greater promotion of EU careers, cooperation with member states, testing in all 24 official EU languages and the competition's accessibility to graduates from any academic discipline.

"Additionally, we have noted the viral spread of messages about the competition in some Member States, which certainly contributed to the competition’s unprecedented visibility," he added.

The traditional assessment centre has been removed, replaced by online reasoning tests, EU knowledge questions, digital skills assessments and a written essay. Testing has also been divided into two stages, with reasoning tests scheduled for this week and the remaining assessments taking place in 2027.

"The decision to organise the tests in two parts was taken to better manage the unprecedented scale of the competition," Salles explained.

EPSO has conducted repeated stress tests with its testing provider, expanded its help desk capacity and upgraded certain platform functions to prepare for the unprecedented number of candidates.

"Although technical issues cannot be ruled out, every effort is being made to minimise potential disruptions," Salles acknowledged.

Previous generalist competitions drew between 21.000 and 51.000 applicants, with numbers falling to around 22.000 in both 2018 and 2019. But this year's total is almost eight times higher than in 2019, with several years' worth of potential candidates competing at once.

The applicant pool also extends beyond people already working in Brussels. According to EPSO, more than 90% of candidates are not currently employed by EU institutions.

Why do EU careers appeal more to some nationalities than others?

Differences in salaries, job security, and employment prospects mostly explain this, particularly in Southern European countries where graduates face more challenging labour-market conditions.

"Interest in EU careers may also be influenced by broader socio-economic factors, such as employment opportunities, labour-market conditions and the attractiveness of public-sector careers in different Member States," Salles told Euronews.

Salary plays a major role. According to Eurostat data, annual net earnings across the EU differ widely. In Luxembourg, net income reached €36,489.56 in 2025, followed by Ireland at €32,052.35 and the Netherlands at €25,750.34. Czechia (€13,107.24) and Estonia (€12,950.21) recorded the lowest amounts.

In some EU countries, real wages have risen only slightly, stagnated, or even fallen in recent decades, while inflation has continued to rise and reduced citizens’ purchasing power. In Spain, wages decreased by 2% between the first quarter of 2021 and the first quarter of 2026. In Czechia, they fell by 5.8%, and in Italy by as much as 6.1%, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) found.

Labour market conditions are the second reason. High unemployment and poor career prospects push people, especially the educated, to apply for higher-paid positions in EU institutions. Spain and Greece, for example, have unemployment rates of 10.3% and 8.1%, respectively, as of May 2026, compared to 3.8% in Germany and 3.9 in the Netherlands.

Beyond pushing up overrepresentation in EU institutions, these issues fuel the so-called "brain drain" phenomenon. The EU Commission says 46 regions are already in the “talent development trap”, meaning they can’t offset the loss of highly educated working-age residents amid depopulation and ageing. These include nearly all of Bulgaria and Romania, Sicily, and parts of Portugal. Another 36 regions, nearly 30% of the EU population, are at risk.

Paul McCartney has joined a very elite club by becoming a billionaire.

McCartney remains active as a musician, most recently releasing his 20th solo album 'The Boys of Dungeon Lane' this year.

In Euronews Culture's review of 'The Boys Of Dungeon Lane', we wrote: "It may not be a late-period masterpiece, but McCartney achieves what he sets out to do: unabashedly embrace the past, take a trip down its long and winding road, and delight in remembrance. McCartney scored his first ever Mercury Prize nomination this year for the album, and in recent news, a huge immersive Beatles fan experience will open in Liverpool in 2028 - one to rival Graceland and Dollywood.

UPDATE, ora 17. După prima zi de discuții trilaterale, secretarul american de Stat, Marco Rubio, a oferit un interviu în care a fost întrebat cum au decurs acestea. Oficialul american a transmis că discuțiile din Emiratele Arabe Unite au fost “foarte productive, însă că mai sunt încă multe de făcut”.

De asemenea, oficialul a mai adăugat că unul dintre obiective este extinderea discuțiilor, pentru a-i putea include și pe europeni. Nu a oferit alte detalii.

Știrea inițială: Noile discuții de la Abu Dhabi vin într-un context diferit. Acestea sunt primele de când SUA și Israelul au lansat atacuri împotriva Iranului și primele după ce republicanii au pierdut alegerile de la jumătatea mandatului. De altfel, acum, Administrația Trump susține că Europa trebuie să participe direct la negocieri. 

Cei doi trimiși ai SUA, Jared Kushner, ginerele lui Donald Trump, și Steve Witkoff, vor încerca să convingă Rusia să accepte prezența europenilor la următoarele discuții. La întâlnirile de la Abu Dhabi sunt prezenți oficiali din Germania, Franța, Marea Britanie și Italia, alături de reprezentanți ai UE și NATO. Este de așteptat, însă, ca aceștia să discute doar separat cu americanii, din cauza opoziției Rusiei, care nu vrea Europa la masa negocierilor. În aceste condiții, europenii sunt îngrijorați că SUA ar putea accepta cererile Rusiei privind reducerea influenței NATO în Europa de Est.

În ceea ce privește pacea, unul dintre planurile Administrației Trump vizează crearea unei noi arhitecturi de securitate între Rusia și Europa. Aceasta ar putea include reluarea Consiliului NATO-Rusia, suspendat după invazia rusă din 2022, precum și ridicarea unor sancțiuni impuse Moscovei. Secretarul general al NATO, Mark Rutte, a participat la discuțiile privind posibilele schimbări.

Șefa diplomației europene, Kaja Kallas, a declarat că Europa are deja acorduri internaționale care garantează suveranitatea și integritatea teritorială a statelor, însă Rusia nu le respectă.

Un alt subiect important îl reprezintă garanțiile de securitate pentru Ucraina. SUA au propus o protecție asemănătoare celei oferite de Articolul 5 al NATO, care prevede sprijinul aliaților în cazul unui atac asupra unui stat membru. În schimb, Rusia se opune aderării Ucrainei la NATO și prezenței trupelor occidentale pe teritoriul acesteia.

Negocierile vor aborda și problema teritoriilor ocupate de Rusia. Donald Trump a sugerat că Ucraina ar putea fi nevoită să renunțe la o parte din teritoriu pentru a ajunge la un acord. În prima zi discuțiile se concentrează pe securitatea Ucrainei și a Europei, iar în a doua zi pe teritorii și stabilirea granițelor.

Ultima rundă de negocieri trilaterale importante dintre SUA, Rusia și Ucraina a avut loc la începutul acestui an, în februarie. După această întâlnire nu au mai existat discuții între cele trei state.

The new power, efficiency and opportunity indices from the World Travel & Tourism Council look at economic strength, environmental efficiency and employment opportunity.

For many years, tourism boards chased one thing, and one thing only: Increased arrival numbers. It didn’t matter how long visitors stayed, or how much they spent, only that the number kept going up and up.

In a world seeing locals pushed out of their own cities by short-term rentals and historic heatwaves causing wildfires and other disruption, there’s been increased focus on sustainable travel.

That means the kind of tourism that both minimises the impact on the environment and benefits local communities – and now there’s a new way to measure this.

The World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) has just launched its new Power, Efficiency & Opportunity (PEO) Indices which evaluates countries based on the environmental impact of tourism, the sector’s contribution to employment, and its economic scale.

“Travel and tourism is one of the world’s most powerful sectors, and these new indices give us a broader and more holistic way to understand its impact,” WTTC president and CEO Gloria Guevara said.

“As the sector grows, we must focus on quality as well as quantity of growth. By assessing economic contribution, environmental efficiency and employment opportunities together, the indices provide valuable insights to support sustainable growth and informed decision-making, while highlighting the sector’s ability to create opportunities for women and young people around the world.”

How do the power, efficiency and opportunity indices work?

The power index is relatively simple, looking at the scale of tourism, employment footprint and levels of tourism investment.

Based on this, the top 10 is made up of the US, China, India, Germany, France, the UK, Japan, Mexico, Spain and Saudi Arabia.

The environmental efficiency index, meanwhile, looks at things like greenhouse gas emissions, low-carbon energy use, water consumption, air pollution and materials use relative to the economic activity tourism generates.

Looking at high-income economies, Sweden ranked the highest on the index, while for upper-middle-income economics, Costa Rica claims the top spot.

Finally, the opportunity index evaluates the sector’s contribution to social development, examining employment growth, youth employment and female employment.

Based on this, Croatia is ranked top for high-income economies; the Maldives for the upper-middle-income group; El Salvador the lower middle income and The Gambia for low-income countries.

Writing about the opportunity index, WTTC notes that in places like the Maldives, Grenada and Belize, tourism supports a significant share of national employment.

Developed by WTTC and Oxford Economics, 184 countries are included in the indices.

Good morning. I’m Luca Bertuzzi, holding the pen for today’s newsletter. In this edition: Merz ties the EU budget to unanimous financial support for Ukraine, Europe sends a delegation to Abu Dhabi but stays outside the trilateral talks, and the Black Sea strategy struggles to stay afloat.

No Ukraine, no budget. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is threatening to block the EU’s next long-term budget unless all member states commit to financing Ukraine beyond 2027, a move that could open a new front in the already fraught MFF negotiations.

Berlin wants governments to agree a durable funding arrangement for Kyiv, including covering the cost of servicing Ukraine-related debt, as Ukraine faces an estimated €70bn funding shortfall next year.

The German leader is not alone in thinking that the EU budget should bring a permanent solution to Kyiv's financial needs. "To have an honest multi-annual budget for Europe, that has to involve considering the question of the funding for Ukraine,” Ireland's Finance Minister Simon Harris said in reply to my colleague Jorge Liboreiro’s question. “Any other conversation would be an incomplete one.”

The EU intends to cover roughly €45bn of the gap, on top of the €90bn Ukraine Support Loan already agreed for 2026-2027. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia opted out of that loan and are not expected to contribute to any top-up. Bulgaria has also signalled it will not contribute further.

However, Merz wrote that the solution should be the result of a “collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly,” suggesting he is opposing additional opt-outs.

Regarding possible opt-outs from a new loan, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said proposals to cover Ukraine’s financing gap should be backed “by the EU27, not by the EU24 or any number of countries”.

At the same time, Germany, which is part of the “frugal” countries seeking cuts to the EU budget, had already tried to tie the budget talks to Ukraine financing at the special European Council at the end of the month, to put pressure on the “Friends of Cohesion”.

In other words, Merz’s gamble raises the stakes further, but it could backfire. Countries that want to opt out of financing Ukraine could feel cornered if they are made to pay for Kyiv and also accept cuts to cohesion funding. In a post-Orbán EU, expect Slovakia’s Robert Fico to play disruptor-in-chief.

Outside of the triangle. The EU will send a joint team of senior officials from the European Commission and the European Council to the US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia taking place today and tomorrow in Abu Dhabi, aiming to secure Brussels a presence in negotiations that could shape the continent’s future security architecture.

The delegation will be led by Björn Seibert, head of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s cabinet, and Anna-Maria Boura, chief foreign policy adviser to European Council President António Costa.

The EU team will be joined by national security advisers from France, Germany and the UK. Italy will also be represented, as part of a wider E4 format, after Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni criticised Rome’s exclusion from the talks. NATO will be represented by Geoffrey Van Leeuwen, chief of staff of NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

The precise format of European participation remains unclear, with the main negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US expected to stay trilateral. European officials have left open the possibility of engaging directly with the Russian delegation, although it is not yet clear whether such a meeting will happen.

"Any meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture can only be undertaken once a ceasefire in Ukraine has been achieved. It must take place in an appropriate forum, in particular with NATO allies and EU members," von der Leyen said at a press conference in Bucharest yesterday, in an indirect reply to US Special Envoy Jared Kushner.

Ukraine’s delegation chief Rustem Umerov has confirmed that Kyiv will hold separate coordination meetings with its European partners in Abu Dhabi.

Sink or swim. Von der Leyen completes her two-day whistlestop tour of Romania and Bulgaria today, seeking to respond to escalating security threats after drone attacks on commercial ships killed seafarers in the Black Sea.

As Angela Skujins writes in, von der Leyen announced on Monday in Bucharest, alongside Romanian President Nicușor Dan, €10m for Romanian search-and-rescue operations. Dan has said the Black Sea will only become truly safe once Russia’s invasion of Ukraine ends.

She also pledged to fast-track the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, with a “clear timeline” for its completion and an additional €50m in dedicated funding. Ironically, she did not provide an exact timeline nor a completion date. The hub is a centrepiece of the Commission’s Black Sea Strategy, published in May 2025.

Former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen told Angela that stronger security in the strategic maritime corridor could follow the Baltic Sea template. “We should set up a maritime mission in the Black Sea to ensure free navigation,” he said.

Iran’s frosty attacks. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, speaking on the sidelines of the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in France, blamed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for last month’s cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators.

The attacks hit thousands of refrigeration units across at least 350 French supermarkets. Barrot said the Iranian ambassador would be summoned and that the issue could prompt further European action.

"If they are attributed, our response should be stronger", EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, indicating that the issue will be on the table of the next Foreign Affairs Council on 16 November.

The ECB package. The President of the European Central Bank, Christine Lagarde, has kicked off the race to succeed her by announcing her resignation a few months ahead of the French presidential elections. In fact, there are two other senior posts at the ECB up for grabs, namely the chief economist and an executive board member.

"This is quite unprecedented," Kyriakos Pierrakakis, Greek Finance Minister and Eurogroup President, told Euronews. "Many see this as a package; I think this is fair," he said, pointing to the need to reach a decision at leaders' level by the end of the year.

The contest for Lagarde's succession is centred around Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands. Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo told Euronews his country's economic performance, with consistent growth, reduction of the debt-to-GDP ratio and investor confidence, gave the candidacy a strong basis.

However, Madrid is heading toward elections this month, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez due to skip the informal European Council in Dublin on Friday. "What we are presenting is a Spanish candidate, not a governmental candidate," Cuerpo said.

UK’s final push. UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds and European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer are in Brussels today to iron out the final details ahead of the UK-EU summit on 20 November.

They will meet Executive Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné and Commissioners Maroš Šefčovič and Andrius Kubilius to discuss industrial cooperation, space and UK-EU supply chains.

Expect the definition of “Made in Europe” to be a sticking point, as London has been pushing to be included in the EU’s local-production regime for public contracts under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act.

Dukes in da hood. There might be even more noteworthy Brits walking around Brussels today, as Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are expected in the European Parliament to attend the opening of Lost Screen Memorial, an exhibition honouring children who lost their lives after experiencing harm on social media.

Europe talks green at COP31 – but scrambles for more fossil fuels

Brussels wants the COP31 to speed up the transition from fossil fuels, but in a world where energy security and affordability are rising up the agenda, more and more governments are seeking short-term oil and gas options.

While European leaders gather at COP31 to discuss how to wean their economies off fossil fuels, many of their governments are scrambling to secure more of them.

The energy turmoil triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran has kept oil and gas at the centre of Europe's economic and geopolitical calculations.

Faced with soaring energy prices, potential supply shortages and mounting pressure from struggling industries, several EU governments are prioritising affordable, reliable energy over longer-term climate commitments – even as delegates at the UN climate summit debate how to phase out fossil fuels.

Although all 27 member states have endorsed the EU's position at COP31, the reality on the ground tells a different story.

The measure was seen as a key test for the global campaign against inequality, but warnings that the super-rich would leave the state won out.

Californians have voted down a proposal for a one-off levy on the state’s billionaires, according to projections by US broadcasters on Monday.

Proposition 40 would have required around 200 of the state’s richest residents to hand over 5% of their total net worth. Most of the money would have gone towards healthcare.

CNN and CBS News both called the result almost a week after polling day. California has the largest population of any US state and is known for counting votes slowly.

The measure had already looked set to fail. With roughly 60% of ballots counted on Wednesday, the “No” side was ahead by 55.6% to 44.4%.

Prop 40 was one of many questions on the ballot in last week’s midterm elections. Those elections brought sweeping gains for the Democrats across the country and heavy losses for President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

Supporters of wealth taxes saw the vote as an important test for a global campaign against widening inequality. If California were a country, it would be the world’s fourth-largest economy, but the gap between its richest and poorest residents is vast.

Campaigners estimated the tax would raise about $100 billion. That money would have gone to the state’s public healthcare system, which has been squeezed by Trump’s budget cuts.

Fears of a billionaire exodus

Opponents spent hundreds of millions of dollars fighting the measure, among them Google co-founder Sergey Brin. They argued it would drive the super-rich out of California.

In the run-up to the vote, “No” campaign adverts filled the state’s TV channels. They warned that California would lose future tax revenue if its billionaires moved elsewhere.

Gavin Newsom, the outgoing governor, had said he would vote against it. Newsom is widely expected to run for the White House in 2028.

Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, sent a statement to AFP through the International Capital Tax Commission before the projections came out. “Significant changes rarely move in a straight line,” he said.

Stiglitz added: “Prop 40 put a tax on billionaire wealth on the ballot in the United States for the first time.”

California has voted on a wealth tax three times before this decade and turned it down each time.

The app was created in Montijo by Carlos Batista, in coordination with this municipality's civil protection, but is intended for all Portuguese people and helps them assemble a "kit" for the first 72 hours after a disaster.

People in Portugal now have an app that can help them follow the European Commission’s recommendation to have an emergency kit ready in case of natural disasters or other emergencies.

The app is called "K72 SMPC Montijo" because it was developed in collaboration with the Municipal Civil Protection Service of Montijo. It is not just for residents of this municipality and can be used by people anywhere in the country.

The K comes from "kit" and "72" refers to 72 hours, the period for which people should have emergency provisions in case a disaster such as an earthquake or flood leaves them trapped. The first 72 hours are considered the most critical phase of an emergency.

The app was developed by Carlos Batista who, besides being a documentary filmmaker, director of photography and drone operator, is also the coordinator of the Local Civil Protection Unit of Montijo and Afonsoeiro.

"The idea came from a desire to create a tool that would not just inform, but push people to take action. There is a lot of information on how to act in emergency situations, but it is not always easy to turn it into concrete measures in our daily lives," says the creator of the app. "I would like K72 to help people take the first step and realise that preparation starts long before an emergency happens," he adds.

André Morais, coordinator of Montijo’s SMPC, stresses that "the challenge is to help each citizen turn what they know into concrete preparedness". In other words, "to think about the risks they are exposed to, agree how to contact family members and know how to act if an emergency disrupts their routines".

Morais says that the goal is not only to get people to assemble the kit, but also to make them talk within the family about what to do in an emergency: "I would like it to lead people to set aside some time to prepare their family. That it would be a reason for a conversation at home: if an emergency happens, do we know what to do? How do we contact each other? Where do we meet? Who needs help?", he says.

With the app, users follow the instructions to put in a backpack the various items they may need in different emergency situations, not only to stay safely at home, but also for evacuation, for the car and even for pets.

In practical terms, the app tells users what to include in each backpack and allows them to mark what they already have and what is still missing. If they have difficulty finding the products, it redirects them to an example item in an online shop.

For example, in the case of an evacuation, the backpack should, according to the app’s creators, contain 45 items that provide shelter and cover, water, food, combustion/fire, cutting tools, ropes and also personal hygiene, medication, communications and power, personal documents and navigation. Through the app, each user marks the articles they already have and those they still need, so they can keep track of the stock in each backpack.

This list of 45 items includes things such as LifeStraw filters and water purification tablets, portable power stations to run electrical devices, or a kit to access the Meshcore network, which allows communication when traditional mobile networks fail.

The K72 SMPC Montijo app also teaches users how to draw up a family emergency plan, serves as a channel for Civil Protection alerts, and includes an inventory that warns when food and medicines in the backpacks are about to expire.

If the worst happens, users can always consult the app for a series of short, precise instructions on what to do in each situation. These include, for example, an urban fire, the presence of toxic gases, an earthquake, heatwaves or cold snaps, prolonged power and water outages, floods and inundations, and more.

The app works with or without internet access, as long as the mobile device has battery power. For privacy reasons, the data each user enters in the app are stored only on the mobile device, with no external database or data sharing.

The creators’ goal is for the K72 app to be used across the country and to help people in Portugal be prepared if or when the worst happens.

In March last year, the European Commission presented a strategy calling for harmonisation between the various member states on strategies for preventing emergency situations. It urges all European citizens to assemble a kit with essential items for survival in the first 72 hours after a disaster, which may be not only a natural catastrophe but also a military attack by a foreign power.

Experts warn that a drop in emissions partly driven by conflict and trade disruptions is not sustainable in the long term.

Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to fall in 2026. The anticipated drop of 0.4 per cent comes as the expansion of renewables accelerates, backdropped by the Iran war energy crisis.

Emissions from oil are projected to decrease by 1.9 per cent, according to the 2026 Global Carbon Budget, which measures progress towards the Paris Agreement goals.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” warns Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study.

But the dip in fossil fuel carbon is offset by a rise in emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation, pushing total CO2 emissions up to a projected 43.3 billion tonnes this year, from 42.8 billion in 2025.

Friedlingstein says further acceleration of renewables and electrification is needed for global emissions to peak and enter a sustained decline.

With electrification central to this week’s COP31 climate talks, global leaders are poised to commit to new targets aligning with this goal.

At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock.

“At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock,” said UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell in his opening remarks on 9 November. “Efficient electrotech and clean energy are a vital cure for planet-heating pollution and spiraling household costs, amid the ongoing fossil fuel cost crisis.”

But experts say progress is still too slow. The remaining ‘carbon budget’ – the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels – is now 150 billion tonnes, equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate, according to the report.

Which countries expect the biggest drop in fossil emissions in 2026?

The EU is projected to see the steepest fall among the major emitters, at 1.5 per cent. The US follows at 1.3 per cent, mainly due to a drop in coal emissions, which spiked last year due to high gas prices and cold weather. Japan’s emissions are set to drop by one per cent.

China is projected to see a 0.9 per cent drop in 2026, thanks to a steep decline in oil emissions and strong growth in renewable electricity generation.

While the country produces 32 per cent of global fossil emissions, it is also a world leader in deploying renewables, as well as reforestation and planting new forests. Half of the global emissions avoided due to renewable energy and electric vehicles are in China.

India bucks the trend, with its emissions projected to rise by 4.4 per cent, above its 3.5 per cent average annual growth over the last decade. The rest of the world is set to see a 0.7 per cent fall, mainly due to higher oil prices and supply constraints.

The report emphasises that decarbonising doesn’t mean sacrificing economic growth: in 2025, 59 countries emitted less than they did before the COVID-19 pandemic, while their economies grew.

Can clean tech offset emissions from growing energy demand?

Two thirds of this year’s rise in global energy demand is being met by solar, wind and electric vehicles, according to the report.

An accompanying analysis by the authors projects that between now and the end of 2028, between 64 and 79 per cent of emissions from new demand will be offset by new solar, wind power and electric vehicles.

Solar and wind helped cut 4.1 billion tonnes of carbon emissions in 2025, up from just 0.28 billion tonnes in 2010. This is projected to reach 4.6 billion tonnes this year.

Electric vehicles are making headway more slowly. Only about 10 per cent of the global car fleet was electrified in 2025, or six per cent excluding hybrids, because the vehicle stock takes time to turn over.

A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change.

“A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change,” says Glen Peters, research professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research and a member of the report’s team. He says clean technologies are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, but not enough to lock in a global peak.

COP31 host Türkiye will push its headline ‘35-by-35’ target at the UN talks, asking countries to collectively raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035. Critics say the target must be met using clean energy if it is to mean anything.

A dip, not a peak in fossil fuel emissions

The picture looks different from last year, when the same report found fossil fuel emissions had hit an all-time high, rising by 1.1 per cent, with oil, gas and coal all increasing.

This year, oil is behind the decline. Emissions from oil are projected to fall by 1.9 per cent and natural gas by 0.3 per cent, while coal is set to rise by 0.6 per cent – likely a short-term response to the energy shock from the Iran conflict rather than a turning point.

Land-use emissions are moving in the opposite direction. They are projected to rise to 5.1 billion tonnes, driven by peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia linked to the onset of El Niño. The report adds that the powerful 2026 El Niño is expected to have a significant impact on the land carbon sink in the coming year.

Carbon removal is also not yet making up the difference. Reforestation and afforestation offset around half of emissions from permanent deforestation, but novel carbon dioxide removal currently offsets less than 30 minutes of annual fossil emissions, according to the report.

Still, the authors say that if the rollout of clean technology keeps accelerating, “a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”

The composition of the Ukrainian and Russian delegations at the Abu Dhabi peace talks offers clues to what could be discussed behind closed doors as US-mediated negotiations resume for the first time in nine months.

Ukraine and Russia will return to the negotiating table in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, nine months after their last round of US-mediated talks. The composition of their delegations offers clues about what each side hopes to achieve.

Kyiv is sticking largely with the same team that took part in previous rounds, signalling continuity in its push for a ceasefire as a first step towards a broader peace agreement.

Moscow, meanwhile, is bringing senior military and diplomatic officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, who helped draft Russia's sweeping security demands to NATO shortly before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

His inclusion raises the possibility that the Kremlin intends to broaden the negotiations beyond Ukraine to Europe's wider security architecture, particularly after US President Donald Trump suggested that an eventual agreement could extend beyond Ukraine.

Ukraine: Continuity in ceasefire push

Ukraine's delegation will again be led by Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, who has played a central role in previous negotiations with Moscow.

He will be joined by Kyrylo Budanov, head of Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the presidential ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction, and Serhii Kyslytsia, first deputy head of the presidential office.

Arakhamia was also in Washington last week, attending a White House meeting hosted by US First Lady Melania Trump on Thursday following the humanitarian ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky.

All four took part in earlier rounds of negotiations, providing continuity as Kyiv seeks to secure a ceasefire and negotiate guarantees against renewed Russian aggression.

Ukraine has repeatedly indicated its willingness to consider different forms of ceasefire, while maintaining that any broader agreement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible security guarantees.

The largely unchanged negotiating team suggests Kyiv intends to maintain that approach rather than substantially revise its position ahead of the renewed talks.

Russia: A familiar face, with significant addition

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin aide and former culture minister who has represented Moscow in previous negotiations with Ukraine.

A staunch supporter of Russia's invasion, Medinsky edited a three-volume textbook, 'Military History of Russia', published in January 2025, which portrays the war in Ukraine as a continuation of the Soviet struggle against Nazi Germany.

Aimed at schoolchildren, the book claims Russia was "forced" to invade Ukraine in February 2022 over NATO’s expansion policy and the 2014 ousting of Ukraine’s pro-Russian president, Viktor Yanukovych, which it labelled "a Western-backed coup".

The three-volume book calls Ukraine an "aggressive anti-Russian bridgehead" and emphasises "battlefield heroism" while pointing at historic parallels between modern Russian military tactics and those of the Soviet army during World War II, which Russia calls "the Great Patriotic War".

In 2014, when Russia first invaded Ukraine, Medinsky, then Russia’s culture minister, issued a document declaring that "Russia is not Europe," arguing that the rest of the continent was morally inferior.

This wasn’t the first time Medinsky tried to show Russia’s superiority to other nations. In 2013, he said that Russia’s "perseverance" in the face of all 20th-century catastrophes indicates that the Russian people "have an extra chromosome".

His return suggests continuity in Moscow's negotiating approach, but the addition of senior diplomatic and military officials raises questions about the scope of the discussions.

Among them is Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, who is joining the Ukraine peace negotiations for the first time.

Ryabkov oversees Russia's relations with the United States, as well as arms control and non-proliferation issues, including those concerning Iran's nuclear programme.

He was closely involved in Moscow's security demands to Washington and NATO in December 2021, shortly before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Those proposals called for an end to further NATO enlargement, including Ukrainian membership, and restrictions on the alliance's military presence in eastern Europe, effectively seeking a rollback to its pre-1997 positions.

Moscow also demanded limits on military exercises and missile deployments, alongside restrictions on nuclear weapons stationed outside their countries of origin.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) has suggested that Moscow could use Ryabkov's experience with those demands to undermine Ukraine's efforts to secure post-war security guarantees.

The US-based think tank also pointed to the negotiating records of other Russian delegates, including Medinsky and Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin, who have previously insisted that any settlement address what Moscow calls the war's "root causes".

ISW argued that the composition of the Russian delegation raised doubts about the Kremlin's willingness to engage in meaningful negotiations.

Ryabkov's participation comes days after US President Donald Trump met Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House on Thursday and suggested that an eventual agreement could extend beyond Ukraine.

"There's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said, adding that it could potentially involve all of Europe.

Although neither Washington nor Moscow has specified whether NATO's wider security arrangements will be on the agenda, Trump's remarks and Ryabkov's appointment have brought renewed attention to the possibility.

Russia is also sending Yuri Zhigarlovsky, deputy head of the General Staff's Main Operational Directorate, which is responsible for military planning and operations.

The Russian delegation met President Vladimir Putin on Friday during a Security Council meeting partly devoted to preparations for the talks.

The presence of senior military and diplomatic officials suggests that discussions could extend across political and security issues, although it remains unclear whether Moscow is prepared to compromise on its longstanding demands.

MWC26 returned to Doha as the industry faces a dual challenge: building the networks that will power artificial intelligence and narrowing a digital divide that still leaves millions of people without mobile internet.

The Middle East and North Africa’s mobile economy is projected to reach €421 billion by 2030, but a new industry report highlights a persistent problem: economic growth is accelerating, yet millions of people still are not benefiting from the digital economy.

GSMA’s Mobile Economy MENA 2026 report, released on the opening day of MWC26 Doha, revealed that mobile technologies and services generated an estimated €340 billion in economic value in 2025, supporting 2.2 million jobs and contributing around €35.8 billion to public finances.

Meanwhile, 48% of MENA’s population used mobile internet last year, while 49% remained offline despite living in areas covered by mobile networks.

The figures point to a challenge that extends beyond infrastructure: ensuring people can afford, access and use the technology available to them.

Doha at the centre of the global connectivity debate

This year’s MWC26 Doha carries added significance as it takes place alongside the International Telecommunication Union’s Plenipotentiary Conference, the first time the two events are being held at the same location.

The two gatherings bring industry leaders and policymakers together at a time when decisions on connectivity standards, digital infrastructure and technological governance will help shape how the global digital economy evolves.

Held in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, the three-day MWC26 Doha aims to advance digital connectivity while also creating meaningful access for consumers.

The event is also being held as the region faces continued uncertainty over the future of the US-Iran war, but opening-day turnout has signalled resilience in the ICT industry and that connectivity remains a business priority.

Building the infrastructure behind the AI boom

As AI systems rapidly evolve to carry out more complex tasks autonomously, the industry faces growing pressure to provide the computing power, capacity and resilience needed to support them.

Speaking at the opening ceremony on Sunday, Qatar’s Minister of Communications and Information Technology, Mohammed bin Ali Mannai, noted the rise of AI agents was increasing the need for more resilient networks and advanced computing capabilities.

For GSMA Director General Vivek Badrinath, the region’s digital future depends not only on expanding connectivity, but also on ensuring networks, services and devices work across borders and communities.

“Progress only counts if everyone shares in it. That means two things: global standards that keep networks, services and devices working across borders, and a concerted effort to connect the people who are still offline,” Badrinath said at the opening ceremony.

Speaking to Euronews, he acknowledged that the industry had not done well in the past year to make mobile connectivity more affordable to the people who really need it.

“A year ago, we were hoping to be able to bring to the market smartphones in the $50 range. That's very much impossible today with the increase of RAM prices driven by the huge demand for AI. This is an unfortunate side effect,” Badrinath said.

He added that strong demand for AI is depriving smartphone producers of the resources they need to make entry-level phones.

Still, investment forecasts are encouraging. GSMA projects that operators will invest around €80 billion across MENA between 2025 and 2030.

But the challenge is ensuring these investments translate into services people and businesses can use.

Quantitative models: AI’s next frontier

While connectivity has become the foundation of most AI functions, the technology is moving fast beyond content generation and chatbots, expanding into fields such as scientific research, healthcare, materials, and energy.

In an interview with Euronews, SandboxAQ CEO Jack Hidary said quantitative AI approaches can help tackle complex problems traditional methods may still struggle to solve.

“The second bucket of AI is AI for the physical world, for the real world. We look at biomedicine, energy, financial services, these big sectors are really areas for LQM and LLMs, so it's great to see the convergence of these two now,” Hidary said.

Fresh from a recent deal with Anthropic and a €449 million R&D award from the US Commerce Department, Hidary believes these milestones will give the company leverage to innovate further.

“It's a very exciting new award that we got to focus on batteries, on magnets, on the things that we need to produce semiconductors in the United States so that we can really power the economy,” he added.

Narrowing the digital divide

Extending network coverage alone will not be enough to prevent the onset of a second digital divide if governments and policymakers do not commit to removing barriers like smartphone affordability, access to data packages, and the skills needed to use digital services.

These barriers risk becoming more consequential as AI reshapes industries and workplaces, impacting people without the tools or training.

Assistant Resident Representative and Inclusive Growth and Innovation Team Leader at UNDP Egypt Abeer Shakweer echoed GSMA’s call for growth that benefits all segments of society.

“Globally, women, persons with disabilities, people in remote and rural areas, and vulnerable young people are at most at risk of being left behind,” she told Euronews in an interview.

Through acceleration programmes that expand access to financial services and new markets, as well as supporting youth at the ideation stage, Shakweer's work at UNDP Egypt helps empower young entrepreneurs and innovators as real contributors to growth.

Ultimately, rapid advancements in the digital economy should not only be about the technology deployed, but about how it gives people the opportunity to shape it, contribute to it, and benefit from it.

Turning connectivity into everyday value

One way connectivity has opened up a tangible pathway for inclusive growth is through financial services.

Mobile wallets and digital payments platforms can give people and businesses new ways to send and receive money, giving merchants a chance to reach more customers and manage transactions more easily.

Mirko Giacco, CEO of Ooredoo Fintech, works at the intersection of connectivity and financial services, tapping into the parent company's vast network while also prioritising underserved communities in the MENA region, such as Tunisia, Oman, the Maldives and Qatar.

“In Qatar, more than 20% of the market share international remittance goes through our products. That means we give users, migrant workers that are here, the tools to send money back home. They do it with us in a way that is safe, convenient, and economically viable,” Giacco told Euronews.

Meanwhile in the Maldives, Ooredoo Fintech has been the first fintech company to enable gig workers to receive payments in US dollars, through a partnership with PayPal.

The GSMA also released a report at MWC26 Doha which looks at how operators in MENA are turning network investments into sustainable returns.

The 5G Monetisation MENA report found that 17 of the region’s 24 markets had launched commercial 5G services by September 2026, while 5G connections are expected to rise from 67 million in 2025 to almost 350 million by 2030.

According to Lonely Planet, the cooler, wetter days mean you’ll have shorter queues at all the big attractions, but the stronger winds also mean excellent windsurfing down the coast in Cascais.

Japan might be better known for its autumn colours, but you’ll find yellow gingko trees and red maple leaves throughout South Korea at this time, too, and without the crowds.

As for February, you can jump on the The Odyssey-inspired set-jetting trend in a sustainable way with a visit to the Peloponnese in Greece. Here, you can visit Ancient Olympia or Ancient Corinth while basking in mild temperatures.

May is all about the Baltics, with Lonely Planet suggesting you embrace the trip-maxxing trend by visiting Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania’s capitals on one break, making use of public transport or by cycling the Baltic Trails network.

Closer to home, Tunisia is an option, particularly as you can take a ferry from European cities including Palermo, Genoa and Marseilles.
